On Potentiality and Actuality Of
Foundation Models

Fabian Gröger    Shuo Wen    Maria Brbić Affiliation: EPFL Email: {fabian.groger,shuo.wen,mbrbic}@epfl.ch
Abstract

Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.

   

1 Introduction

The rapid progress of foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021) has been driven by large-scale pre-training on general-domain data, often followed by post-training and finally adaptation to a specific task, behavior, or domain. To adapt these models effectively, different adaptation strategies have been explored. The earliest form of adaptation is full fine-tuning, which updates all model parameters on a given task (Howard and Ruder, 2018; Devlin et al., 2019). To reduce computational cost, parameter-efficient methods freeze the model and learn only a small update, such as the widely used low-rank update of LoRA (Hu et al., 2022; Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021). In-context learning showed that it is possible to adapt by eliminating parameter updates altogether and instead conditioning the model on demonstrations in the prompt (Brown et al., 2020). Similarly, activation steering leaves the model parameters unchanged, but adapts model behavior at inference time by directly modifying hidden activations (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023). So far, the field has largely treated these adaptation strategies as different tools suited for different settings.

But what is the underlying mechanism of adaptation, and what changes inside a foundation model when it gains task-specific expertise? While these questions remain largely unanswered, a growing body of evidence suggests that task adaptation may rely on small changes to a pre-trained model. In particular, fine-tuning succeeds when the update is restricted to a small parameter space (Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022), or even when it is restricted to biases with a new task layer (Ben Zaken et al., 2022) or to 0.01%0.01\% of the weights (Panigrahi et al., 2023). Recent work on neural thickets even showed that random perturbations of pre-trained weights find dense sets of diverse task experts (Gan and Isola, 2026). Why such small interventions are sufficient to produce task-specific expertise remains poorly understood. Previous work has suggested that we are in the elicitation overhang: AI models have untapped capabilities, and we do not know how to elicit them from frontier models (Turner et al., 2023).

To understand the adaptation mechanism, we first decompose the update that LoRA learns into two components: (i) a component shared across all inputs, and (ii) an input-specific component, i.e., a residual that varies with the input. Across many diverse tasks, we find that most of the adaptation gain can be reached without input-specific adaptation: the update vectors point in nearly the same direction independent of the input. Quantitatively, on 26 benchmarks and 18 language models from 7 architecture families, the component shared across all the inputs preserves 85%85\% of the adapted behavior. Motivated by this finding, we adapt the model via shift adapter, a simple adaptation mechanism that learns only the shared part of adaptation: a single vector per layer, constant for every input. Since the update a shift adapter learns is added unchanged to every input, unlike the update of LoRA, bias-only training, or full fine-tuning, every difference between the answers to two inputs is computed by the frozen base model. The shift adapter matches LoRA’s performance across 17 tasks and 18 language models, with roughly two orders of magnitude fewer parameters. The same holds for adaptation without the rank constraint and for full fine-tuning, where the savings are even larger.

These findings suggest that the base model itself already has the capacity for diverse task-specific expertise and only a small push in the right direction is needed to put this capacity to work. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models, and the push towards a direction to gain task-specific expertise the actualization of a foundation model. The terms reflect Aristotle’s distinction between potentiality (dunamis), a capacity that a thing holds without exercising it, and actuality (energeia), that same capacity at work (Aristotle, ca. 350 B.C.E.). In this terminology, a pre-trained foundation model holds different task-specific expertise as potentiality, and that expertise can be actualized via a constant shift that moves the model into a state where it can be exercised (Figure 1).

The potentiality and actuality principle has implications on fine-tuning, steering, neural thickets, and model convergence. It provides an explanation for why fine-tuning can succeed in a tiny parameter space (Aghajanyan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Ben Zaken et al., 2022; Sinii et al., 2025), identifies the trained shift as a reference direction for steering (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023), relates the dense task experts found by random perturbations to states that actualize existing capacities (Gan and Isola, 2026), and shows that the states of different models grow alike as the models gain capability (Huh et al., 2024; Gröger et al., 2026). In each case the mechanism is the same: a state that actualizes a capacity the model already has.

2 Shared and input-specific components of adaptation

Imagine that a foundation model already holds the task-specific expertise in potentiality and that adaptation only has to actualize it by selecting the desired expertise. In such a case, the selection would be the same for every input of the task, i.e., the update learned during adaptation would not vary across inputs, or would vary only slightly.

To test this hypothesis, we split the change that adaptation does into two components: (i) a component shared by all the inputs, and (ii) an input-specific component. We measure how much of each component changes during adaptation, and evaluate the model using only one of the two components to determine which component the adaptation relies on. We explore this for different kinds of adaptation: LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), the same update trained without the rank constraint (the unconstrained update), full fine-tuning (Howard and Ruder, 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), and in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020).

Adaptation field. Every form of adaptation changes the hidden states that the model computes for an input, whether it updates the weights or places demonstrations in the prompt. We thus describe adaptation through this change. Let hℓbase​(x)∈ℝdh^{\mathrm{base}}_{\ell}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and hℓadapted​(x)∈ℝdh^{\mathrm{adapted}}_{\ell}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the hidden states after layer ℓ\ell of the base and the adapted model for input xx, where dd is the hidden size. We define the adaptation field at layer ℓ\ell as their difference and decompose it into a component shared by all inputs, its mean, and an input-specific component,

ℱℓ​(x)=hℓadapted​(x)−hℓbase​(x)=ℱ¯ℓ⏟shared component+ℱ~ℓ​(x)⏟input-specific component,ℱ¯ℓ=𝔼x​[ℱℓ​(x)].\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(x)=h^{\mathrm{adapted}}_{\ell}(x)-h^{\mathrm{base}}_{\ell}(x)=\underbrace{\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}}_{\text{shared component}}+\underbrace{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}(x)}_{\text{input-specific component}},\qquad\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(x)]. (1)

The shared component ℱ¯ℓ\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell} is one vector per layer, the same for every input. The input-specific component ℱ~ℓ​(x)\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}(x) has zero mean over inputs, so the two components add in energy (Proposition B.1),

𝔼x​∥ℱℓ​(x)∥2=∥ℱ¯ℓ∥2+𝔼x​∥ℱ~ℓ​(x)∥2.\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(x)\rVert^{2}=\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}\rVert^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}(x)\rVert^{2}. (2)

We quantify the decomposition with two statistics (Figure 2, Section C.7): (i) the share of the field’s energy that the shared component holds defined as ∥ℱ¯ℓ∥2/𝔼x​∥ℱℓ​(x)∥2\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}\rVert^{2}/\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(x)\rVert^{2} (the first term of Equation 2 over its left side), which we call the field share, and (ii) the average cosine between each input’s field ℱℓ​(x)\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(x) and the shared component ℱ¯ℓ\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell}. The cosine similarity is close to 1 if adaptation moves every input in the same direction and close to 0 if it moves each input differently.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). In LoRA adaptation, a low-rank update Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA is added to each weight matrix W∈ℝdout×dinW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}, which maps a dind_{\mathrm{in}}-dimensional input to a doutd_{\mathrm{out}}-dimensional output, with B∈ℝdout×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r}, A∈ℝr×dinA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} and rank r≪min⁡(din,dout)r\ll\min(d_{\mathrm{in}},d_{\mathrm{out}}). We adapt every linear projection in every layer, the common choice (Dettmers et al., 2023; Biderman et al., 2024), and consider one adapted matrix WW at a time, since the derivation is the same for each. Let zt​(x)∈ℝdinz_{t}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} be the hidden state that WW multiplies at token position tt for input xx. The base model computes W​zt​(x)Wz_{t}(x) and the adapted model (W+Δ​W)​zt​(x)(W+\Delta W)z_{t}(x), so what LoRA adds at this matrix is the vector at​(x)=Δ​W​zt​(x)∈ℝdouta_{t}(x)=\Delta Wz_{t}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}. Unless stated otherwise, we take ztz_{t} at the last token of the input, where the model has read the entire input and is about to answer, and drop the index tt. Because Δ​W\Delta W is linear, the added vector can be split into the shared and input-specific component:

a⁡(x)=Δ​W​z​(x)=Δ​W​μ⏟shared component+Δ​W​(z⁡(x)−μ)⏟input-specific component=a¯+a~​(x),a(x)=\Delta Wz(x)=\underbrace{\Delta W\mu}_{\text{shared component}}+\underbrace{\Delta W\bigl(z(x)-\mu\bigr)}_{\text{input-specific component}}=\bar{a}+\widetilde{a}(x), (3)

where μ=𝔼x​[z⁡(x)]∈ℝdin\mu=\mathbb{E}_{x}[z(x)]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} is the average hidden state estimated on held-out inputs the adapter has never been trained on.

Experimental setup. We apply the decomposition to trained LoRAs of rank 88, on 18 models from 7 architecture families: 14 instruction-tuned, 3 base models, and 1 trained on instructions but not preference-tuned (Section C.2). Each model is adapted on 26 benchmarks from two categories: (i) 17 reasoning and knowledge tasks with labeled answers which test what the model knows and how it reasons, and (ii) 9 behaviors including 4 traits which ask for the answer in a given language, persona, or format, 3 transformations which ask the model to apply a specific rule to the input, and 2 maps, a letter cipher and a lookup table, which assign each input an answer by an arbitrary rule. Nothing in pretraining fixes that rule, so the maps are the one category the model can only learn from the adaptation data. We refer to the first category as tasks, and the second as behaviors. The tasks span commonsense reasoning, text classification, subject-specific question answering, and recent complex reasoning benchmarks (e.g., BoolQ, HellaSwag, MMLU-Pro, and SuperGPQA), following the protocol of Hu et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024b) (details Section C.3). Tasks are evaluated by accuracy on their evaluation splits, while behaviors are evaluated on 1,0001{,}000 held-out generations by adherence to the target behavior. For each intervention, we report the fraction of the adaptation gain over the base model that is retained. Unless stated otherwise, results are averaged over 3 seeds.

Observation. Across 17 tasks and 18 models, each input’s field points along the shared component at a cosine of 0.910.91 on average, and the shared component holds 83%83\% of the field’s energy (Figure 3a, all models in Section D.2). Across the 9 behaviors and 18 models, the cosine is 0.840.84 and the shared component holds 71%71\% of the field’s energy (Section D.5). The same decomposition applies to the adapter’s own output a⁡(x)=Δ​W​z​(x)a(x)=\Delta Wz(x), before it propagates through the model. There the shared component a¯\bar{a} holds 89%89\% of the energy on these behaviors and 89%89\% on the tasks, averaged over every adapted matrix (Section D.3). The fields of different inputs thus point in nearly the same direction: LoRA moves every input mostly the same way, and the part of the change that depends on the input holds the smaller share of the energy on both tasks and behaviors.

Interventions. We next explored which component the LoRA gains come from using two interventions: (i) keeping only the shared component, and (ii) removing the shared component. In the first intervention, the same shared vector a¯\bar{a} replaces a⁡(x)a(x) in Equation 3 at every adapted matrix and at every position so the adapter becomes one constant vector per matrix. In the second intervention, a¯\bar{a} is subtracted at every position, so the model relies only on the input-specific component a~​(x)\widetilde{a}(x). The former tests whether the shared component alone produces the adapted behavior on new inputs, while the latter tests whether the trained adapter depends on the shared component.

Over all 18 models, keeping only the shared component keeps on average 85%85\% of the adapter’s gain on the tasks, and removing it keeps 61%61\% (Figure 3b, Figure 12). Two other ways of removing it keep 84%84\% and 75%75\% (Section D.2), so on the tasks each component alone can produce most of the gain. All models keep more with the shared component alone than without it. The only exception is Mistral-7B, which relies on both components about equally. The 3 models that never received instruction tuning keep 85%85\% of the gain with only the shared component and 59%59\% with it removed, against 87%87\% and 63%63\% on the instruction-tuned models, so the reliance on the shared component is not a product of instruction tuning (Section D.4). The same holds for behaviors, where the shared component alone keeps 86%86\% of the gain on average, and removing it keeps 33%33\% on the traits, 57%57\% on the transformations, and 26%26\% on the maps. The update matters while the model reads the input, not while it writes the answer: with the adapter switched on only for the input tokens, LoRA keeps 83%83\% of its gain, and only for the answer tokens 12%12\%, on 18 models and 6 tasks (Section D.7). So most of what LoRA gains comes from one vector per matrix that is the same for every input, added while the model reads the input.

We next ask whether adaptation still relies on a shared component when producing the correct behavior requires input-specific computation. The 3 transformations, such as copying the input or returning its last word, apply a rule to the input that the base model can already follow, so the computation that varies with the input is the model’s own. Surprisingly, even there, keeping only the shared component keeps 92%92\% of the gain, as much as on the 4 traits, which ask for the same behavior on every input (88%88\%, Figure 3c). The 2 maps apply a rule fixed by an arbitrary key, a substitution of the first letter, or a table of words, which the model can only learn during adaptation, and they keep the least, 74%74\% of adaptation gain. This indicates that gains of the shared component fall when the base model does not hold the rule. On the maps, what adaptation adds is the table, and what the base model provides is the ability to use one: a shift adapter trained on a map answers as well as LoRA does, and the table it stores produces nothing on its own (Section E.5).

Unconstrained update. To investigate the influence of the low-rank update on the decomposition result, we train the same update without the low-rank factorization, so that Δ​W\Delta W is a full matrix at every adapted matrix, on the same 18 models, the 4 traits, and the 3 transformations. After training, the update has high rank (median stable rank 4747** * Stable rank is ∥W∥F2/∥W∥22\lVert W\rVert_{F}^{2}/\lVert W\rVert_{2}^{2}, the squared Frobenius norm over the squared spectral norm.) and raises adherence as much as LoRA does (0.440.44 against 0.430.43 above the base model), yet its shared component holds 95%95\% of the energy of what it adds, against LoRA’s 90%90\%. Without the shared component, it keeps 26%26\% of the adaptation gain on traits and 49%49\% on transformations, against LoRA’s 39%39\% and 59%59\%. With the shared component alone, it keeps 69%69\% against LoRA’s 87%87\% on traits (Section D.9). The shared component is therefore not a product of the low-rank constraint: with the constraint gone, it grows from 90%90\% of the energy to 95%95\%, while the behavior relies on it slightly less.

Fine-tuning and ICL. We further examine whether full fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) rely on the shared component in the same way LoRA does. Full fine-tuning changes every weight, so its update cannot be decomposed and intervened on as LoRA’s. However, we can examine the structure of its adaptation field: we find that adaptation via fine-tuning results in nearly the same shared structure as LoRA. Across the 17 tasks and 18 models, its cosine is 0.900.90, and its field share is 0.810.81 on average, compared to 0.910.91 and 0.830.83 for LoRA (Section E.2), suggesting that all inputs are moved in the same direction, just like we observe for LoRA. In contrast, ICL relies more on input-dependent changes: its shared component keeps less of the gain than LoRA’s on traits, transformations and tasks, and its shared component remains nearly orthogonal to LoRA’s even as their induced hidden-state changes become more aligned in later layers (Section D.10). This suggests that ICL reaches similar behaviors through a different, more input-dependent route. Additional results are in Appendix D.

3 Actualizing with a shift adapter

In the previous section, we showed that we can preserve most of the adaptation gain by keeping only the component shared across the inputs. If this shared component is indeed sufficient to produce the adapted behavior or solve a task, then we should be able to learn such a change directly. We therefore define a shift adapter: one learned vector bℓ∈ℝdb_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} per layer ℓ\ell, added to the hidden state of every input at every position. Its only operation is a constant push. The shift applies the same push to every input and moves the model into a state in which its expertise for one task is actualized. We call such a state an actualizing state. Note that a constant parameter does not mean a constant effect: the layers above process the push together with an input-dependent hidden state, so the same push can move different inputs differently, and they can reach different actualizing states. However, the capacity to move inputs differently lies in the base model, and the shift only actualizes it via a constant push. This sets the shift adapter apart from LoRA, bias training and full fine-tuning, which can change the output of a block differently for each input (Section B.3). This gives an operational distinction: a capacity is actualized when a constant vector suffices on inputs never seen in training, and memorized when the gain holds only on the items seen in training (Sections E.6 and F.12).

Shift adapter matches LoRA. We compare the shift adapter to LoRAs of rank {1,4,8,16,64}\{1,4,8,16,64\} on the 17 tasks across 18 models, with the training and evaluation protocol of Section E.1. The shift reaches a mean accuracy of 0.7460.746, against 0.7450.745 for a LoRA of rank 8 and 0.6200.620 for the base model (Figure 4a), recovering all of the LoRA’s gain, with L×dL\times d trainable parameters, 0.040.04M on Qwen2.5-1.5B compared to 9.29.2M for LoRA with rank 8. The same holds at every rank: from rank 11 to rank 6464 the LoRA’s accuracy moves by 0.0030.003 while its parameters grow from 1.21.2M to 7474M on that model. The shift stays within 0.0120.012 of the rank-8 LoRA on any task and within 0.0110.011 on any model, from 0.50.5B to 2626B parameters (Figure 4b,c). Training all weights reaches 0.7180.718 under the protocol above, so the shift adapter is above full fine-tuning on every model.

The shift and LoRA agree on the actualizing direction. The shift adapter and LoRA are trained independently, so we next wondered whether they push the inputs along the same direction and finally reach the same actualizing state. Across the 17 tasks and 18 models, the average cosine similarity of LoRA’s shared component and the shift adapter is 0.640.64 on average, while a LoRA with random weights gives 0.060.06 (Section E.4). Across the 9 behaviors and 18 models, the cosine similarity is 0.530.53 on average, while a LoRA with random weights gives 0.070.07 compared to the shift adapter (Figure 5). Every bar sits above its random counterpart: a LoRA with random weights reaches 0.840.84 on the tasks and 0.660.66 on the behaviors for the cosine to its own shared component, and only 0.060.06 and 0.070.07 for its cosine to the trained shift (Figure 5). If, instead of weighting each layer equally as before, we weight each layer by how far the shift adapter moves it, cosine similarity rises to 0.690.69, and the random LoRA remains at 0.080.08 (Section C.7). The comparable performance and similar direction of the shift adapter and LoRA indicate that LoRA relies on the direction the shift adapter learns, even though it can vary its update with every input. Additional results are in Appendix E.

4 The structure of actualization

All these results indicate that the base model already holds task-specific expertise in potentiality, and adaptation can rely on a constant input-independent push to reach the state in which task-specific expertise can be actualized. Together they form the two parts of the potentiality and actuality principle: (i) the base model holds the task-specific expertise in potentiality, and (ii) a constant shift can actualize the task-specific expertise of the base model. In this section, we aim to better understand this principle. In particular, we aim to understand when, during training, the potentiality forms in the base model, and what geometry the actualizing region has.

When during training potentiality forms. If the base model holds the task-specific expertise in potentiality and a shift actualizes it, when during training does the potentiality form? We investigate this question in OLMo-2-7B (Team OLMo et al., 2025), which has intermediate public checkpoints. Specifically, we look at 15 checkpoints spanning its training: 5 from stage-one pretraining on Dolma (Soldaini et al., 2024) between 11B and 3,8963{,}896B tokens, 6 from the 5050B-token stage two, and 4 released base, supervised, preference-tuned, and instruct models. At every checkpoint we repeat the comparison of Section 3 and the decomposition of Section 2, on the 17 tasks (Section F.1).

The analysis shows that the potentiality already forms during pretraining, at different points for different kinds of tasks (Figure 6). Text classification comes first, the shift adapter raises the base model’s accuracy on the 3 classifications from 0.570.57 to 0.860.86 already at 99B tokens. Science question answering, the domain tasks, sentence completion, and expert question answering arrive far later, and until 105105B tokens the adapted model does no better than answering with the most frequent label. So the potentiality forms in the base model during stage-one pretraining, at different points for different kinds of tasks, and once a kind of task-specific expertise has formed, the shift actualizes it at every later checkpoint, through stage two and post-training alike.

From 99B tokens on, the shift and the rank-8 LoRA reach accuracy within 0.010.01 of each other at every checkpoint, so the shift matches LoRA once the expertise has formed. Only at 11B tokens does the rank-8 LoRA score slightly higher than the shift (Section F.1). For behaviors, the potentiality principle forms later: at 99B tokens a rank-8 LoRA produces 4040 to 4242 of the 4242 writing systems (non-Latin scripts such as Thai), where a shift produces 77 to 88, and the two meet only at 105105B tokens (Section F.2, F.11). The shift adapter fails at 99B tokens because the capacity has not yet formed: at this checkpoint the trained LoRA itself does not rely on its shared component, which alone produces none of the writing systems, while at 105105B tokens the same shared component alone produces 3737 to 4040 of them and a shift adapter 3838 to 4141 (Section F.11). A shift adapter thus reaches a behavior from the point at which pretraining has formed the capacity, and LoRA starts to rely on its shared component from about the same point. Pythia-12B shows the same order across its pretraining checkpoints (Section F.3). On the 17 tasks, the LoRA relies on its shared component at every checkpoint: with only that component it keeps between 70%70\% and 93%93\% of its gain at the 15 checkpoints, from 11B tokens to the instruct model (Table 10). So pretraining forms the task-specific expertise, and adaptation actualizes it through the component shared by all inputs, which remains the same from the first checkpoint on.

What geometry does the actualizing region have. We characterize an actualizing region by three properties: (i) width in magnitude, (ii) width in direction, and (iii) connectivity. Across the 9 behaviors of the setup on 18 models, we measure width in magnitude by scaling a trained shift and width in direction by rotating it away from its trained direction. The region is narrow in magnitude but wider in direction: at least 90%90\% of the gain is preserved between 0.80×0.80\times and 1.34×1.34\times the trained magnitude and up to a 34∘34^{\circ} rotation, while half is preserved between 0.61×0.61\times and 1.86×1.86\times and up to 50∘50^{\circ} (Figure 7, Sections F.6 and F.7). Directional width depends on what the shift is rotated toward: on the 4 traits, rotating toward another trait’s shift reduces the 90%90\% and 50%50\% thresholds to 13∘13^{\circ} and 26∘26^{\circ}, respectively (Section F.8). We measure connectivity by interpolating between independently trained states for the same behavior. Specifically, we train the same behavior at 3 seeds, take two of the resulting states, and score the shift at 5 equally spaced points on the straight line between them. Across the 9 behaviors and 18 models, the lowest point along the interpolation retains a median 99%99\% of the endpoint gain, indicating that the two states lie in a single connected region, with the gain remaining high along the entire interpolation path. Connectivity also holds when the two states are trained from different supervision sources: one from the model’s system-prompted answers and the other from externally translated answers, across French, German, and Spanish. This shows that actualizing states of the same behavior lie in connected regions, not in separate pockets (Section F.9). We next assessed whether the size of the region correlates with the performance. Indeed, larger measured regions show stronger behaviors: across the 9 behaviors and 18 models, region area correlates with adherence at the center at within-model Spearman +0.64+0.64 (Section F.10).

5 Implications of the potentiality and actuality principle

We examine implications the potentiality and actuality principle has on (i) steering, (ii) convergence, and (iii) neural thickets.

Implications on steering. Activation steering (Subramani et al., 2022) provides a direct example of the potentiality and actuality principle: adding an appropriate direction in activation space can actualize a desired behavior without changing the model’s weights. However, the challenge for steering is to identify the right actualizing direction. Existing steering methods extract such directions from model activations (Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023; Beaglehole et al., 2026), but the resulting interventions can be sensitive to how the direction is constructed and how strongly it is applied. Instead of extracting the direction heuristically, the shift adapter learns the actualizing shift directly from behavioral examples. We compare three extracted vectors, the mean difference of CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024), the leading principal component of the same differences (Zou et al., 2023), and the in-context task vector (Hendel et al., 2023), with the shift adapter on the 9 behaviors and 18 models. Following standard practice (Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023), we choose the strength on 200200 held-out instructions and evaluate all methods on 800800 further instructions. The shift adapter reaches an adherence of 0.680.68 against 0.170.17 for the best of the three extracted vectors, on average over 18 models with intervals over models, and it leads in every class: 0.450.45 against 0.200.20 on the traits, 0.870.87 against 0.100.10 on the transformations, and 0.830.83 against 0.230.23 on the maps (Figure 8a). We further evaluate on AxBench (Wu et al., 2025), where the shift adapter scores 0.870.87 compared with 0.210.21 for CAA on Gemma-2-2B (Section G.2). In this view, activation steering is one way of actualizing what the model already holds. However, it often fails to find the right actualizing state. The shift adapter instead reliably actualizes the desired state.

Implications on convergence. The Platonic representation hypotheses (Huh et al., 2024) observes that the representations of different models grow alike as the models grow more capable. The potentiality and actuality principle raises the same question for the states a model can be brought to: do the actualizing states of different models converge, and does the agreement grow with capability? A state is named by the behavior it produces, so the state for answering in French in one model has a partner in every other model that answers in French, and we can compare how two models arrange their states just as we compare how they arrange their representations (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Kornblith et al., 2019). We train one shift adapter for each of the 7575 behaviors that 1414 instruction-tuned models all reach, each behavior with a name and a system prompt (languages, output forms of the kind IFEval verifies (Zhou et al., 2023), personas of the kind persona vectors control (Chen et al., 2026), and eras, registers, affects and audiences, Section C.4), and compare the arrangements of the 7575 states between all model pairs with RSA (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008), which compares the rank order of the angles between states, CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019), which compares their inner products up to a rotation and a scale, and mutual-kkNN (Huh et al., 2024), which compares which states are nearest neighbors. To know what agreement two unrelated arrangements show, we shuffle which behavior is which in one of the two models and score the shuffled pair the same way (Gröger et al., 2026). The states of different models show high agreement: RSA between models of different families is 0.640.64, every pair lies above its shuffled counterpart (p<0.01p<0.01), and the more capable the two models, the closer their arrangements under RSA (Spearman ρ=0.68\rho=0.68, p=0.003p=0.003) and mutual-kkNN (ρ=0.40\rho=0.40, p=0.03p=0.03), while CKA does not rise with capability (Figure 8b, Section G.3). In this view, models converge not only in what they compute for a given input but in what they hold in potentiality, and they converge more the more capable they become.

Implications on neural thickets. Gan and Isola (2026) recently showed that adding random perturbations to the weights of the large pretrained model can yield task-improving experts. In large models, the density of such experts is high: a substantial fraction of random weight perturbations improve performance on a task. However, why such task-improving experts become abundant around pretrained weights is an open question. The potentiality and actuality principle offers a way to explain this phenomenon: an expert is a perturbation that happens to land in the actualizing region of the task, i.e., the region in which the behavior can be actualized. A perturbation of fixed size lands in the actualizing region and finds experts by chance only when the actualizing regions are wide, and none when the regions are narrow. To test this, we first reproduce the random-search protocol of Gan and Isola (2026) on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and then run it on the 9 behaviors of our setup, whose actualizing regions we measured in Section 4. Following Gan and Isola (2026), we sample 300300 random weight perturbations at several noise scales, keep the 2020 that score highest on a selection set, and evaluate those on a disjoint held-out set. We call the share of the 2020 that still improve the behavior on the held-out set the expert fraction. On the GSM8K the search finds experts in 12 of the 18 models, with an expert fraction of 0.200.20 on average. Across model-behavior pairs, expert density increases with actualizing-region size. In the 8 models where the search finds an expert, the behaviors with an expert have wider regions than those without: region size and expert density correlate at Spearman ρ=0.43\rho=0.43 over the 72 model–behavior pairs (p<0.001p<0.001, Section G.4), and the share of pairs with an expert rises from 0%0\% in the narrowest quarter of regions to 17%17\% in the widest (Figure 8c). The three behaviors with the narrowest regions have no expert in any model. Thus, neural thickets can be understood as random search entering actualizing regions by chance: the wider the region, the more likely it is to contain randomly discovered experts.

6 Related work

The potentiality and actuality principle connects different adaptation strategies through the states they induce. More details are in Appendix A.

Parameter-efficient and representation fine-tuning. Parameter-efficient methods restrict adaptation to low-rank updates (Hu et al., 2022), biases with a new task layer on linguistic classification tasks (Ben Zaken et al., 2022), updates over frozen factors (Zhang et al., 2023), or updates restricted to particular subspaces (Gao et al., 2024). Representation-based methods instead modify hidden states directly, from input-dependent low-rank updates in ReFT (Wu et al., 2024) to fixed offsets at selected attention heads in LoFiT (Yin et al., 2024). Each of these updates can change the output of a block differently for each input: the biases of Ben Zaken et al. (2022) sit inside the block, so their change passes through attention and the MLP (Section B.3), while the shift adapter adds its vector after the block. Moreover, 13/18 models we evaluate have no biases at all, making bias training not applicable. Sinii et al. (2025) train one vector per layer with reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning and see its input-independence as a limitation, while we find that most of what LoRA adds is the same for every input. The potentiality and actuality principle shows that a constant, input-independent shift is sufficient to move the model into a state in which task-expertise can be actualized.

In-context learning. In-context learning adapts through demonstrations (Brown et al., 2020). Prompt tuning, prefix tuning, and gisting learn that conditioning instead of supplying it (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021; Mu et al., 2023). Our comparison reveals a different route from LoRA: the demonstrations’ shared component keeps less of the gain than LoRA’s on traits, transformations and tasks, and is nearly orthogonal to LoRA’s shared component.

Activation steering. Activation steering modifies hidden states using directions extracted from activation contrasts (Subramani et al., 2022; Rimsky et al., 2024) or their principal components (Zou et al., 2023). We compare extracted directions with the shift adapter added at the same place in the model and find it reaches behaviors that steering misses.

From weight updates to actualizing states. Wang et al. (2025) show that single-layer LoRA updates in out-of-context reasoning point in nearly the same direction across tokens, and that extracted or trained steering vectors can induce the learned behavior. Adila et al. (2026) derive a local first-order relation between weight updates and activation shifts and build post-block activation adapters. Our paired intervention tests this correspondence in trained, multi-layer LoRAs: keeping only the shared component tests its sufficiency, while removing it tests the update’s reliance on it.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we explore what adaptation does to a foundation model. By disentangling the shared and input-dependent components of adaptation, we find the potentiality and actuality principle: adaptation primarily actualizes expertise already present in the model. The shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that trains a single input-independent vector per layer reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. This principle provides a common perspective on parameter-efficient fine-tuning, activation steering, convergence across models, and neural thickets, and connects adaptation through weights, prompts, and hidden representations as different routes to actualizing model capabilities.

Appendix A Extended related work

Adaptation strategies differ in what they change: parameter-efficient fine-tuning learns a small update to the weights, in-context learning conditions the model on demonstrations in the prompt, activation steering modifies the hidden activations at inference time, and representation fine-tuning learns a change to the representations themselves. The field has treated these as different tools. The potentiality and actuality principle reads each of them as reaching an actualizing state.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the model and trains a small update to its weights. The update can be a low-rank matrix on selected weights (Hu et al., 2022), the existing biases and a new task layer (Ben Zaken et al., 2022), per-feature scales over frozen random factors (Kopiczko et al., 2024), one LoRA factor with the other left random (Zhu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023), or an update confined to a random, Fourier, shared or gradient subspace (Gao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2024; Mandica et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2025). Low intrinsic dimension is the broadest form of the observation that so little suffices (Aghajanyan et al., 2021). Grafting the fine-tuned values of 0.01%0.01\% of the weights, chosen by a learned sparse mask, onto the base model keeps over 95%95\% of the fine-tuned accuracy, and in a model tuned on several tasks at once the tasks use nearly disjoint sets of weights (Panigrahi et al., 2023). That work finds which weights carry the gain and in which layers and modules they sit. Each such weight still multiplies the input, so its effect on the hidden states could differ from input to input. For LoRA and full fine-tuning we find the opposite: most of the gain lies in a component shared by all inputs (Section 2). We show why it suffices: the update selects a state the base model holds in potentiality, and the shift adapter, one vector per layer, is the smallest member of this family that does so (Section 3).

In-context learning. In-context learning adapts a model through demonstrations in the prompt, with no change to the weights (Brown et al., 2020), carried by attention heads that copy from the context (Olsson et al., 2022). Mechanism work compresses the demonstrations into a single vector: a task vector read from the hidden state at the end of the prompt (Hendel et al., 2023), or a function vector read from a small set of attention heads, which reproduces the task when added to the forward pass (Todd et al., 2024). The prompt itself can also be learned: prompt tuning trains the embeddings of a few tokens placed before the input (Lester et al., 2021), prefix tuning trains such tokens at every layer (Li and Liang, 2021), and gisting trains the model to compress a long prompt into a few tokens that stand in for it (Mu et al., 2023). We place in-context learning beside adaptation on the same behaviors and find that it reaches them by a different route: its shared component keeps less of the gain than LoRA’s on the traits, the transformations and the tasks, and it points nearly orthogonally to LoRA’s shared component (Section 2). The task vector is then one of the three extracted vectors we compare with the trained shift adapter in Section 5.

Activation steering. Activation steering adds a vector to the hidden states at inference time and leaves the weights untouched. The vector comes from the model’s own activations: Activation Addition takes the difference between the activations of two prompts (Turner et al., 2023), Contrastive Activation Addition averages that difference over many prompt pairs with and without the behavior (Rimsky et al., 2024), Representation Engineering reads the leading direction of such differences (Zou et al., 2023), and persona vectors apply the same construction to character traits (Chen et al., 2026). AxBench benchmarks these methods against fine-tuning on one fixed model, Gemma-2-2B, with its own judge (Wu et al., 2025). The trained shift adapter adds its vector at the same place, one per layer, but learns it by adaptation, and Section 5 shows that training reaches behaviors that extraction misses.

Representation fine-tuning. Representation fine-tuning trains a change to the hidden representations and leaves the weights frozen. ReFT learns a low-rank transformation of the representations at chosen positions, which in general depends on the input (Wu et al., 2024). LoFiT learns fixed offsets at a few selected attention heads (Yin et al., 2024). Bias training trains the existing biases together with a new classification layer for each task, through which every answer leaves the model (Ben Zaken et al., 2022), and Sinii et al. (2025) train a bias vector per layer with reinforcement learning to match fully tuned reasoning models on mathematical benchmarks, a bound on how few parameters reasoning needs. They see the input-independence of this vector as a limitation that may cap performance, while our paper shows that most of what LoRA adds is the same for every input (Section 2) and explains why such a vector suffices (Sections F.11 and F.12). The new layer of Ben Zaken et al. (2022) adds an input-specific component trained on the task, so accuracy there cannot show that the expertise was already in the base model. The vector of a shift adapter is the shared component of what any adaptation learns, on which a LoRA relies for most of its gain (Section 2).

From weight updates to actualizing states. Wang et al. (2025) study single-layer LoRAs on out-of-context reasoning tasks and find that the update’s added vectors point in nearly the same direction across tokens, and that extracted or directly trained steering vectors can induce the learned behavior. Adila et al. (2026) derive a local first-order relation between weight updates and activation shifts and use it to build post-block activation adapters. Both connect changes in weights to states in activation space. Our paired intervention turns this correspondence into a test of the trained update itself: keeping only the shared component and removing it establish when a flexible multi-layer LoRA relies on an actualizing state (Section 2).

Table 1 summarizes what each of these works shows and the questions about adaptation that our paper adds.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 The shared and input-specific decomposition

Proposition B.1 (A linear update adds a shared component plus a low-rank input-specific component).

Let zz be a random vector with mean μ\mu and covariance Σ\Sigma, and let the adapter add a⁡(z)=Δ​W​za(z)=\Delta Wz with rank⁡(Δ​W)≤r\operatorname{rank}(\Delta W)\leq r. Then

a⁡(z)=a¯+a~​(z),a¯=Δ​W​μ,a~​(z)=Δ​W​(z−μ),a(z)=\bar{a}+\widetilde{a}(z),\qquad\bar{a}=\Delta W\mu,\qquad\widetilde{a}(z)=\Delta W(z-\mu),

Cov⁡(a~​(z))=Δ​W​Σ​Δ​W⊤,rank⁡(Δ​W​Σ​Δ​W⊤)≤r,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\widetilde{a}(z)\right)=\Delta W\Sigma\Delta W^{\top},\qquad\operatorname{rank}\!\left(\Delta W\Sigma\Delta W^{\top}\right)\leq r,

and the energy identity of Equation 2 holds.

Linearity gives Δ​W​z=Δ​W​μ+Δ​W​(z−μ)\Delta Wz=\Delta W\mu+\Delta W(z-\mu), and 𝔼⁡[Δ​W​(z−μ)]=Δ​W​𝔼​[z−μ]=0\mathbb{E}[\Delta W(z-\mu)]=\Delta W\mathbb{E}[z-\mu]=0. 𝔼⁡[Δ​W​(z−μ)​(z−μ)⊤​Δ​W⊤]=Δ​W​Σ​Δ​W⊤,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Delta W(z-\mu)(z-\mu)^{\top}\Delta W^{\top}\right]=\Delta W\Sigma\Delta W^{\top},

𝔼​∥Δ​W​z∥2=∥Δ​W​μ∥2+2​(Δ​W​μ)⊤​𝔼​[Δ​W​(z−μ)]+𝔼​∥Δ​W​(z−μ)∥2.\mathbb{E}\lVert\Delta Wz\rVert^{2}=\lVert\Delta W\mu\rVert^{2}+2(\Delta W\mu)^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\Delta W(z-\mu)]+\mathbb{E}\lVert\Delta W(z-\mu)\rVert^{2}.

Remark B.2 (The decomposition is the intervention).

Keeping only a¯\bar{a} and keeping only a~​(z)\widetilde{a}(z) are the two interventions of Section 2. The proposition gives an exact split into the two components, and the interventions measure which one the adapted behavior relies on.

Lemma B.3 (The frozen layers supply the input dependence).

Let Gℓ:ℝd→ℝmG_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be differentiable and let bℓ∈ℝdb_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be fixed. For every input xx, the local effect of adding bℓb_{\ell} to hℓ​(x)h_{\ell}(x) is

dd​α​Gℓ​(hℓ​(x)+α​bℓ)|α=0=JGℓ​(hℓ​(x))​bℓ.\frac{d}{d\alpha}G_{\ell}\!\left(h_{\ell}(x)+\alpha b_{\ell}\right)\bigg|_{\alpha=0}=J_{G_{\ell}}\!\left(h_{\ell}(x)\right)b_{\ell}. (4)
