B.3 Bias training is not a shift adapter

Prior work on bias training adapts a model by training its existing bias terms (Ben Zaken et al., 2022). The shift adapter instead adds one new vector at the output of each block, the same for every input and every position. Both train few parameters and reach the accuracy of larger updates, so to position the two works we ask whether they are the same parameterization. They are not. The biases of our models act inside attention, before the softmax and the MLP of the same block, so a change of them changes the output of the block differently for each input. The shift adapter adds the same vector to the output of the block for every input. Below we show which biases our models have and what a change of each bias can affect, and then formally show that no change of a block’s attention parameters, its biases included, reproduces a shift adapter.

Bias terms of our models. Thirteen of our 18 models have no bias terms at all (Table 2), so bias training has no parameters to train on them. The other five are the Qwen2.5 models, which have biases only on the query, key, and value projections of attention. No model has a bias at the output of a block or at the output of its MLP, which is where the shift adapter is placed. On most of the models in this paper, bias training thus does not exist, while the shift adapter applies to every model, and where both exist, they differ in placement.

What a change of each bias can affect. Let u1,…,uTu_{1},\dots,u_{T} be the normalized hidden states that enter attention at the TT positions of an input. For one head, attention computes at every position jj a query, a key, and a value,

qj=WQ​uj+bQ,kj=WK​uj+bK,vj=WV​uj+bV,q_{j}=W_{Q}u_{j}+b_{Q},\qquad k_{j}=W_{K}u_{j}+b_{K},\qquad v_{j}=W_{V}u_{j}+b_{V},

and its output at position ii is a weighted average of the values,

ai=WO​∑j≤iαi​j​vj,αi​j=softmaxj⁡(1d​qi⊤​kj),a_{i}=W_{O}\sum_{j\leq i}\alpha_{ij}\,v_{j},\qquad\alpha_{ij}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\,q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}\Big),

where the weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} of each position sum to one. Bias training changes bQb_{Q}, bKb_{K}, and bVb_{V}. We change one of them by a vector δ\delta, keep all other parameters fixed, and follow the change through the block (Figure 9a).

  • •

    Query bias, bQ→bQ+δb_{Q}\to b_{Q}+\delta. Every query becomes qi+δq_{i}+\delta, so the score between positions ii and jj changes by (Ri​δ)⊤​Rj​kj/d(R_{i}\delta)^{\top}R_{j}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}, with the rotary embeddings described for the key bias below. The key kjk_{j} depends on the input at position jj, so the attention weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} change, and they change differently for different inputs.

  • •

    Key bias, bK→bK+δb_{K}\to b_{K}+\delta. Every key becomes kj+δk_{j}+\delta, so the score changes by qi⊤​δ/dq_{i}^{\top}\delta/\sqrt{d}. Without rotary embeddings this is the same for every jj, and the softmax removes it. Our models use rotary embeddings (Su et al., 2024), which rotate the query and the key by angles that depend on their positions, qi↦Ri​qiq_{i}\mapsto R_{i}q_{i} and kj↦Rj​kjk_{j}\mapsto R_{j}k_{j}. The change of the score is then (Ri​qi)⊤​Rj​δ/d(R_{i}q_{i})^{\top}R_{j}\delta/\sqrt{d}, which differs between positions jj and depends on the input through qiq_{i}.

  • •

    Value bias, bV→bV+δb_{V}\to b_{V}+\delta. Every value becomes vj+δv_{j}+\delta. Since the weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} sum to one, the output of attention changes by WO​δW_{O}\delta at every position, the same vector for every input. This vector, however, is added to the hidden state before the MLP of the same block. The MLP then receives hi′+WO​δh^{\prime}_{i}+W_{O}\delta instead of the hidden state hi′h^{\prime}_{i} after attention, and how much its output changes depends on hi′h^{\prime}_{i}, and so on the input.

In all three cases, the output of the block changes by an amount that depends on the input. The shift adapter instead adds its vector bb after the MLP, to the output hi′′h^{\prime\prime}_{i} of the block, where nothing in the block acts on it. The block output then changes by the same vector bb for every input (Figure 9b).

Notation. We now show formally that this holds for every change of attention, not only for a change of its biases. We treat one pre-norm block (Xiong et al., 2020) as a function of its input H=(h1,…,hT)H=(h_{1},\dots,h_{T}), the hidden states at the TT positions, each of dimension d≥2d\geq 2. We consider every input whose hidden states are nonzero, not only the inputs that a prompt produces, because the proof scales inputs up. Let

  • •

    Norm\mathrm{Norm} be the RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), applied to each hidden state. It divides a vector by its root mean square, so scaling a vector does not change its normalized form: Norm⁡(λ​h)=Norm⁡(h)\mathrm{Norm}(\lambda h)=\mathrm{Norm}(h) for every λ>0\lambda>0.

  • •

    U=Norm⁡(H)U=\mathrm{Norm}(H) be the normalized input, and Attnt​(U)\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U) the output of attention at position tt. Attention, including its rotary embeddings and its causal mask, sees the input only through UU.

  • •

    MLP\mathrm{MLP} be the MLP of the block. Our models use gated MLPs with the smooth activations SiLU or GELU (Shazeer, 2020), so the MLP is differentiable.

We write g⁡(y)=MLP⁡(Norm⁡(y))g(y)=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{Norm}(y)) for the output of the MLP on a hidden state y≠0y\neq 0. It is differentiable, and like Norm\mathrm{Norm} it does not change when yy is scaled: g⁡(λ​y)=g⁡(y)g(\lambda y)=g(y) for every λ>0\lambda>0. We assume that gg is not constant, since an MLP that gives the same output for every input would play no role.

The block and its field. Like every transformer block (Vaswani et al., 2017), the block adds the output of attention and the output of the MLP to its input, through the residual connection (He et al., 2016):

ht′=ht+Attnt​(U),ht′′=ht′+MLP⁡(Norm⁡(ht′)).h^{\prime}_{t}=h_{t}+\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U),\qquad h^{\prime\prime}_{t}=h^{\prime}_{t}+\mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{Norm}(h^{\prime}_{t})\big).

A change of the parameters of attention, whether of its biases, its weights, or a LoRA on them, turns Attn\mathrm{Attn} into Attn+Δ​Attn\mathrm{Attn}+\Delta\mathrm{Attn}. We now follow this change through the block in three steps.

  1. 1.

    After attention, the hidden state becomes ht′+Δ​Attnt​(U)h^{\prime}_{t}+\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U).

  2. 2.

    The MLP receives this changed hidden state, so the block output becomes

    h~t′′=ht′+Δ​Attnt​(U)+MLP⁡(Norm⁡(ht′+Δ​Attnt​(U))).\tilde{h}^{\prime\prime}_{t}=h^{\prime}_{t}+\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U)+\mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{Norm}(h^{\prime}_{t}+\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U))\big).
  3. 3.

    The change of the block output, the field at position tt, is the difference to the unchanged output ht′′h^{\prime\prime}_{t}:

    Ft​(H)=h~t′′−ht′′=Δ​Attnt​(U)⏟change of attention+MLP⁡(Norm⁡(ht′+Δ​Attnt​(U)))−MLP⁡(Norm⁡(ht′))⏟change it causes in the MLP.F_{t}(H)=\tilde{h}^{\prime\prime}_{t}-h^{\prime\prime}_{t}=\underbrace{\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U)}_{\text{change of attention}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{Norm}(h^{\prime}_{t}+\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U))\big)-\mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{Norm}(h^{\prime}_{t})\big)}_{\text{change it causes in the MLP}}.

A shift adapter with vector bb at this block turns ht′′h^{\prime\prime}_{t} into ht′′+bh^{\prime\prime}_{t}+b, so its field is Ft​(H)=bF_{t}(H)=b at every position and for every input. A change of attention reproduces a shift adapter exactly when its field is such a constant vector. The proposition shows that this never happens.

Proposition B.4 (No change of attention acts as a shift adapter).

In the setting above, suppose that a change of the attention parameters of a block gives the same field Ft​(H)=bF_{t}(H)=b at every position tt and for every input HH. Then b=0b=0, and the change of attention has no effect. Hence no change of the attention parameters of a block, its biases included, acts as a shift adapter at the output of that block.

Proof idea. Scaling the input up leaves attention unchanged and makes the two MLP terms cancel, so attention itself must add bb. The MLP then has to give the same output whether or not bb is added before it. For a nonzero bb, this means that the output of the MLP does not change when its input moves in the direction of bb. Since scaling the input does not change it either, the MLP would give the same output everywhere, which it does not.

Proof.

Suppose that Ft​(H)=bF_{t}(H)=b for every input HH and every position tt. Fix HH and tt, and write a=Attnt​(U)a=\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U) and Δ=Δ​Attnt​(U)\Delta=\Delta\mathrm{Attn}_{t}(U). With gg, the field reads

Ft​(H)=Δ+g⁡(ht+a+Δ)−g⁡(ht+a)=b.F_{t}(H)=\Delta+g(h_{t}+a+\Delta)-g(h_{t}+a)=b. (1)

Step 1: attention itself adds bb. Replace HH by λ​H\lambda H with λ>0\lambda>0. Its hidden states are still nonzero, so (1) holds for λ​H\lambda H. The normalized input UU does not change, so aa and Δ\Delta do not change either, and hth_{t} becomes λ​ht\lambda h_{t}. Since gg does not change when its argument is scaled, we can divide both arguments by λ\lambda, and (1) for λ​H\lambda H reads

Δ+g⁡(ht+(a+Δ)/λ)−g⁡(ht+a/λ)=bfor every ​λ>0.\Delta+g\big(h_{t}+(a+\Delta)/\lambda\big)-g\big(h_{t}+a/\lambda\big)=b\qquad\text{for every }\lambda>0. (2)

As λ\lambda grows, both arguments of gg tend to hth_{t}, which is nonzero, and gg is continuous there. The two gg terms therefore cancel in the limit, and Δ=b\Delta=b. Since HH and tt were arbitrary, the change of attention adds the same vector bb for every normalized input and at every position.

Step 2: the MLP does not change along bb. Insert Δ=b\Delta=b into (2), cancel bb on both sides, and write ε=1/λ\varepsilon=1/\lambda:

g⁡(ht+ε⁡(a+b))=g⁡(ht+ε​a)for every ​ε>0.g\big(h_{t}+\varepsilon(a+b)\big)=g\big(h_{t}+\varepsilon a\big)\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0. (3)

Subtract g⁡(ht)g(h_{t}) on both sides and divide by ε\varepsilon. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the left side tends to the derivative of gg at hth_{t} in the direction a+ba+b, and the right side to the derivative in the direction aa. Because gg is differentiable, this derivative is linear in the direction, so the two sides differ by the derivative in the direction bb, which must therefore be zero. Every nonzero vector xx can be the hidden state hth_{t} of some input (place xx at position tt and any nonzero vectors elsewhere), so

the derivative of gg at xx in the direction bb is zero, for every x≠0x\neq 0. (4)

Step 3: a vector the MLP ignores is zero. Suppose that b≠0b\neq 0, and take any xx that is not on the line through 00 and bb. The points x+s​bx+sb, for real ss, then never reach 00, and by (4) the function s↦g⁡(x+s​b)s\mapsto g(x+sb) has derivative zero everywhere. It is therefore constant, so g⁡(x+s​b)=g⁡(x)g(x+sb)=g(x) for every s>0s>0. Since gg does not change under scaling, g⁡(x+s​b)=g⁡(x/s+b)g(x+sb)=g(x/s+b), which tends to g⁡(b)g(b) as ss grows. Hence g⁡(x)=g⁡(b)g(x)=g(b) for every xx off the line of bb. A nonzero xx on that line is the limit of the points x+w/nx+w/n off the line, for any w≠0w\neq 0 orthogonal to bb, so g⁡(x)=g⁡(b)g(x)=g(b) there too, by continuity. Then gg gives the same output for every nonzero hidden state, which contradicts our assumption. Hence b=0b=0, by Step 1 the change of attention is zero, and the field is zero for every input. ∎

What the proposition covers.

  • •

    Methods. It covers every change of the attention parameters: its biases, as in bias training, its weights, a LoRA on its projections, and the offsets of LoFiT (Yin et al., 2024), which add a fixed vector to the output of selected heads before the output projection. None of them acts as a shift adapter.

  • •

    Models. It applies to the pre-norm blocks of 16 of our 18 models. The other 2, the Gemma-2 models, also normalize the output of attention and of the MLP before adding it to the residual stream. They have no bias, so bias training does not apply to them.

  • •

    Earlier blocks. A change of the biases of an earlier block reaches this block only through its input. The proposition applies to the block that holds the changed parameter.

The proof treats the RMSNorm as exactly scale invariant. In practice a constant of 10−610^{-6} is added to the mean square for numerical stability, which at the hidden-state norms of our models changes the normalization by less than one part in 10910^{9}. The proof also uses that the MLP is differentiable, which holds for the gated MLPs of all 18 models.

Appendix C Experimental protocol

C.1 The setup

Unless a subsection states otherwise, every experiment uses the setup of Section 2: the 18 models of Section C.2, the 26 benchmarks of Table 3 (17 tasks and 9 behaviors) and 3 training seeds. Every method trains at the learning rate selected for it (Section C.5). A run is one model, benchmark, method and seed, so a benchmark contributes 54 runs per method. Every reported number is the mean over the seeds, and every interval a 95%95\% bootstrap interval over models. Tasks are scored on their full evaluation split and behaviors on 1,0001{,}000 held-out generations per run. A subsection that departs from this setup, in its models, benchmarks, seeds or evaluation size, states its own design in its first paragraph.

C.2 Models

The text experiments use 18 models from 7 architecture families. Fourteen are instruction-tuned: Qwen2.5-0.5B, 1.5B, 3B and 7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, Qwen3.6-27B, Llama-3.2-1B and 3B, Llama-3.1-8B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Mistral-7B and Gemma-2-2B. Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 interleave three gated linear-attention blocks with every full-attention block, so the models are not one architecture repeated at different scales. Four further models are read before preference tuning (Section D.4): the base models behind Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-2B, and Tulu-3-8B-SFT (Lambert et al., 2025), which is trained on instructions but not preference tuned. The convergence analysis in Section 5 uses the 14 instruction-tuned models.

C.3 Benchmarks

Table 3 lists the 26 benchmark datasets: 17 tasks and 9 behaviors, including 4 traits, 3 transformations and 2 maps.

C.4 Behavior sets for the convergence analysis

Each behavior of the convergence analysis is a system prompt. In each model a shift adapter is distilled for every behavior on the same 160160 instructions for 300300 steps. The analysis runs on the 7575 behaviors that every atlas holds (Table 4).

C.5 Instructions, teachers and training

Instructions and teachers. Every trait is trained and scored on instructions from the no-context part of dolly-15k (Conover et al., 2023), about 1515k instructions of 2020 to 160160 characters with duplicates removed. Each seed draws its own training instructions, and the held-out instructions a behavior is scored on never overlap the ones it trained on. The number of instructions is fixed within each experiment for every model and method it compares, and follows how many states the experiment trains. A behavior of the setup trains on 8080 instructions for 250250 steps, and a map on 160160 for 400400, so that every first letter occurs in training. An atlas, which trains hundreds of behaviors per model, uses 160160 for 300300 steps, as do the in-context comparison and the behavior counts along the training of OLMo-2-7B. A region grid, which scores hundreds of points around one state, uses 6060 for 300300, and the steering comparison uses 400400 for 200200. The teacher is the base model under a system prompt for a trait, and the rule itself for a transformation or a map.

Objective and defaults. The adapter (a shift adapter or a LoRA) is trained on the teacher’s answers to bare prompts: the loss is next-token cross-entropy on the answer tokens only, with instruction and padding tokens masked, and AdamW updates the adapter parameters alone. The default rates are 10−310^{-3} for shift adapters and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} for LoRA, and on the tasks the rate chosen by the selection below, for 250250–800800 steps per behavior and a batch of 44 unless stated. Figure 11 shows the training and held-out loss curves of one model on one trait. Loss is a diagnostic: every claim is scored on generated text (Section C.6).

Learning-rate selection. For the 17 tasks of Figure 4 the learning rate is selected per model, adapter, and task with the same procedure, so that no adapter is compared at a tuned rate against another at an untuned one. For each task we split the training data in two: a validation part and the rest. Every rate is trained on the rest and scored on the validation part, and the rate that scores highest is kept, ties within 0.0050.005 going to the smaller rate. The adapter is then retrained on the full training data at that rate, for every seed. The evaluation split is never used for selection, and no rate carries from one task to another. The rates are {1,5}×10−5\{1,5\}\times 10^{-5}, {1,5}×10−4\{1,5\}\times 10^{-4}, {1,2,5}×10−3\{1,2,5\}\times 10^{-3} and 10−210^{-2} for the shift adapter, {1,2,5}×10−5\{1,2,5\}\times 10^{-5} and {1,2,5}×10−4\{1,2,5\}\times 10^{-4} for LoRA, and {3×10−7,10−6,3×10−6,10−5,3×10−5,10−4}\{3\times 10^{-7},10^{-6},3\times 10^{-6},10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},10^{-4}\} for full fine-tuning.

Parameter counts. Adapter sizes depend on the model’s depth LL, its width dd and the adapted matrices mm. A shift adapter trains L×dL\times d parameters, 0.040.04M on Qwen2.5-1.5B, and a rank-rr LoRA trains r​∑m(din(m)+dout(m))r\sum_{m}(d^{(m)}_{\mathrm{in}}{+}d^{(m)}_{\mathrm{out}}), 9.29.2M for r=8r{=}8 on the same model.

C.6 Evaluation

Every claim is scored on generated text for held-out instructions, never on teacher-forced loss. The format behaviors (bullet points, all caps, JSON, one word and socratic) are scored by a rule-based verifier, as the adapted rate minus the base model’s rate. Every other trait is scored by the token-F1 similarity of the generation to the teacher’s generation, minus the same similarity for the base model. We call this score adherence. Transformations and maps are scored by exact match.

Direct checks of the language and persona scores. We rescore the saved generations of the interventions of Section 2 with a direct measure, without new training or generation. A frozen 9797-language identifier finds the target language in under 1%1\% of the base model’s answers and in 67%67\% to 100%100\% of the trained adapter’s, on every one of the 18 models. Counting an answer as French when the identifier labels it French, across the 18 models, keeping only the shared component keeps 99%99\% of the gain and removing it keeps 16%16\% (medians over runs), close to the token-F1 values. A lexical marker gives the same ordering for the personas: with only the shared component, pirate keeps 99%99\%. The result on the languages does not depend on token F1. Token F1 scores a generation by its overlap with the teacher’s answer. A different wording of the same behavior scores low. The direct checks above read the behavior itself, and they give the same ordering.

C.7 Field statistics

For nn probe inputs, the cosine and the field share of Section 2 at layer ℓ\ell and position tt are

Cℓ,t=1n​∑i=1n⟨ℱℓ,t​(xi),ℱ¯ℓ,t⟩∥ℱℓ,t​(xi)∥​∥ℱ¯ℓ,t∥,Eℓ,t=∥ℱ¯ℓ,t∥2n−1​∑i∥ℱℓ,t​(xi)∥2.C_{\ell,t}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\langle\mathcal{F}_{\ell,t}(x_{i}),\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell,t}\rangle}{\lVert\mathcal{F}_{\ell,t}(x_{i})\rVert\,\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell,t}\rVert},\qquad E_{\ell,t}=\frac{\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\ell,t}\rVert^{2}}{n^{-1}\sum_{i}\lVert\mathcal{F}_{\ell,t}(x_{i})\rVert^{2}}.

A layer-averaged value weights every layer the same, and averages only the layers the adapter reaches: the field is zero at the embedding output, where Cℓ,tC_{\ell,t} is undefined, and including those layers would lower every method’s cosine by about 0.070.07. The cosine between two shared components, cos⁡(ℱ¯ℓ,tA,ℱ¯ℓ,tB)\cos(\bar{\mathcal{F}}^{A}_{\ell,t},\bar{\mathcal{F}}^{B}_{\ell,t}) of Figure 5, is averaged the same way. Weighting each layer by how far the adapter moves it, ∥ℱ¯ℓ,tA∥​∥ℱ¯ℓ,tB∥\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}^{A}_{\ell,t}\rVert\lVert\bar{\mathcal{F}}^{B}_{\ell,t}\rVert, changes no ranking and sharpens both comparisons: on the 9 behaviors and 18 models, the shift adapter, the LoRA and a random LoRA reach 0.790.79, 0.780.78 and 0.560.56 against the unweighted 0.850.85, 0.840.84 and 0.660.66, and the shift adapter against the LoRA’s shared component reaches 0.690.69 where a random LoRA stays at 0.080.08. A layer where either component is near zero has no direction to compare, which is what the weighting removes.

C.8 Intervals

Unless a subsection states otherwise, brackets are bootstrap 95%95\% intervals that resample models (Section C.1), and a subsection that resamples runs, tasks or concepts says so. A plain range (aa to bb) is a minimum and a maximum over the stated models. Where per-probe scores are available, we report the interval over runs beside a bootstrap over probes within runs (Section D.8).

The comparison of models (Section G.3) uses 9191 pairs of models. Each model appears in 13 pairs, so the pairs are dependent, and we attach no pp-value that assumes independence to their correlation with capability: that result uses a permutation of model labels that preserves the pairs, and 2,0002{,}000 permutations of behavior labels per pair calibrate each pair’s similarity.

Appendix D Shared and input-specific components

D.1 The two interventions

The two interventions of Section 2 are reported as fractions of the adapter’s gain over the base model. For an adaptation AA whose added vector can be isolated, and a held-out score SS, accuracy or adherence, we define

RkeepA=S⁡(Amean)−S⁡(base)S⁡(A)−S⁡(base),NmeanA=S⁡(A)−S⁡(Aremove​mean)S⁡(A)−S⁡(base).R_{\mathrm{keep}}^{A}=\frac{S(A_{\mathrm{mean}})-S(\mathrm{base})}{S(A)-S(\mathrm{base})},\qquad N_{\mathrm{mean}}^{A}=\frac{S(A)-S(A_{\mathrm{remove\ mean}})}{S(A)-S(\mathrm{base})}. (5)

The fraction of the gain kept with only the shared component is RkeepAR_{\mathrm{keep}}^{A}, and the fraction kept with it removed is 1−NmeanA1-N_{\mathrm{mean}}^{A}. Over a set of runs, each fraction is a ratio of sums, the summed gain that remains over the summed gain, and it takes every run, so a run with a small gain carries little weight. A fraction for a single run divides by that run’s own gain, so a median over runs (Section D.7) uses only the runs whose gain reaches 0.050.05. Figure 3 draws both fractions.

D.2 Interventions and field statistics on the tasks

We apply the two interventions to the rank-8 LoRAs trained on the 17 tasks of Section C.3, on the 18 models. Each intervention is scored by accuracy on the task’s full evaluation split, and the shared component is estimated from 300300 held-out probes. Figure 3b draws one model per family, and Figure 12 draws every model.

With only the shared component, the LoRA keeps 85%85\% [8181, 8989] of its gain, and with it removed 61%61\% [5252, 6969]. The LoRA gains less than 0.050.05 in 325325 of the 918918 runs, most of them on MedMCQA, SciQ, the two ARC sets, SST-2 and SIQA, and these runs carry little weight in the ratio of sums. Per task, the fraction kept with only the shared component ranges from 66%66\% on HellaSwag to 99%99\% on DBpedia, and the fraction kept with it removed from 17%17\% on ARC-Easy to 88%88\% on AG News. By task type, with intervals over models, the fractions kept with only the shared component and with it removed are 97%97\% [9696, 9898] and 59%59\% [4646, 7171] on the three text classifications, 87%87\% [8383, 9090] and 58%58\% [5050, 6666] on the four commonsense question-answering tasks, 78%78\% [7070, 8787] and 49%49\% [1818, 7474] on the three science question-answering tasks, 79%79\% [7373, 8585] and 73%73\% [6464, 8282] on the four domain tasks, 66%66\% [4545, 7979] and 61%61\% [3131, 7777] on HellaSwag, and 69%69\% [6060, 7676] and 66%66\% [5858, 7575] on the two expert question-answering tasks, MMLU-Pro and SuperGPQA. The shared component alone keeps at least 66%66\% of the gain on every task type.

Two checks concern how the fractions are measured. First, estimating the shared component as the average input of the matrix over all prompt positions, instead of at the last token of the input, keeps 70%70\% [6666, 7373] of the gain with only that component and 93%93\% [9191, 9494] with it removed. The gain relies on the component the adapter adds at the last token of the input, on the tasks as on the traits (Section D.8). Second, macro accuracy stays close to accuracy: within 0.0370.037 on those runs, and on the setup’s runs, each scored under the trained adapter and the two interventions, within 0.040.04 in all but 4 of the 2,7542{,}754 reports (at most 0.0830.083, under removal), with a mean gap of 0.000.00. No fraction comes from predicting the majority class.

Removing the shared component position by position. The interventions estimate one shared component at the last token of the input and apply it at every position. To test what the earlier positions share, we estimate a second shared component over the positions before the last token, on the same held-out probes, and remove each component where it was estimated: (i) the component estimated over the prompt from the prompt positions, and (ii) the component estimated at the last token from that token. Across the 18 models and 17 tasks, removing both in this way keeps 84%84\% of LoRA’s gain, against 61%61\% when the single component is removed at every position. Removing the direction of the shared component, by projecting the field at every position onto the subspace orthogonal to it so that nothing the adapter adds points along it, keeps 75%75\%. Each of the 3 removals leaves a different part of the update, and each keeps more than half of the gain.

The two methods solve the same items. Matched accuracy does not tell whether the shift adapter and LoRA solve the same held-out items. On the 17 tasks and 18 models, we take the items the base model gets wrong and compare the ones each method newly solves. Of the items one method newly solves, the other newly solves 82%82\% (median over the runs), against 51%51\% if the two methods picked their items at random from the base model’s failures. In 916916 of the 918918 runs (one per model, task, and seed), the observed share is above this chance level. It is above chance on every one of the 17 tasks (Figure 13a), and most clearly on the harder tasks, such as MedMCQA (68%68\% against 22%22\%) and ARC-Challenge (74%74\% against 30%30\%). Chance is high only where both methods solve almost every item the base model gets wrong, as on DBpedia, since two nearly complete sets of items always overlap. Per model, it runs from 73%73\% on Mistral-7B to 91%91\% on the Llama-3.1-8B base model (Figure 13b). Two seeds of one method agree on the items to the same degree: of the items one seed of the shift adapter newly solves, another seed solves 85%85\%, and for LoRA 82%82\%. The shift adapter and LoRA thus solve the same items as closely as one method does across its own seeds.

D.3 The shared component inside the adapter

The interventions act on what the adapter adds at each adapted matrix, a⁡(x)=Δ​W​z​(x)a(x)=\Delta Wz(x), so its decomposition in Equation 3 can be measured directly, without the hidden states. For each adapted matrix we compute the share of the energy of what the adapter adds that its shared component holds, ∥a¯∥2/𝔼x​∥a⁡(x)∥2\lVert\bar{a}\rVert^{2}/\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert a(x)\rVert^{2}, the field share of Section 2 applied to aa in place of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Over every adapted matrix of the runs on the 9 behaviors and the 18 models, the shared component holds 89%89\% of the energy on average (median 96%96\%), from 66%66\% on the Gemma-2-2B base model to 99%99\% on SmolLM2-1.7B. For the update without the rank constraint the median is 98%98\% (Section D.9). At almost every adapted matrix, LoRA adds nearly the same vector for every input.

We repeat this measurement on the 17 tasks and the 18 models, and the result is the same: at almost every adapted matrix, LoRA adds nearly the same vector for every input. The shared component holds 89%89\% of the energy on average (median 98%98\%), from 82%82\% on Tulu-3-8B-SFT to 93%93\% on Qwen3.6-27B, and between 97%97\% and 98%98\% for every kind of matrix (Figure 14a). The share stays above 99%99\% in the first tenth of the layers and falls only toward the last layers, to 92%92\% for the query, key, and value matrices and to 8484 to 87%87\% for the output and MLP matrices in the last tenth (Figure 14b). The part of the update that differs between inputs is thus small, and it is concentrated in the last layers.

D.4 Models before instruction tuning

Instruction tuning could be what makes adaptation rely on a shared component. We test this on the 3 models that never received instruction tuning: the base models behind Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-2B. They run on the same 17 tasks. With only the shared component, the LoRA keeps 85%85\% [8282, 9292] of its gain, and with it removed 59%59\% [2525, 7070], against 87%87\% [8484, 9191] and 63%63\% [5353, 7272] on the 14 instruction-tuned models. Per model, the fraction kept with only the shared component is 84%84\% for Llama-3.1-8B, 92%92\% for Qwen2.5-7B and 82%82\% for Gemma-2-2B.

On the 9 behaviors, the same 3 models keep 81%81\% [7676, 9090] of the gain with only the shared component and 55%55\% [5151, 5959] with it removed, against 87%87\% [8080, 9292] and 39%39\% [2929, 4949] on the 14 instruction-tuned models. Per model, the fraction kept with only the shared component is 76%76\% for Llama-3.1-8B, 90%90\% for Qwen2.5-7B and 78%78\% for Gemma-2-2B (Figure 12b). Adaptation relies on the shared component before instruction tuning, on tasks and behaviors alike.

D.5 Interventions on the traits and transformations

We apply the two interventions to LoRAs trained on the 4 traits and the 3 transformations. What the LoRA adds at an adapted matrix is a⁡(x)=Δ​W​z​(x)a(x)=\Delta Wz(x). Keeping only the shared component replaces it by a¯=Δ​W​μ\bar{a}=\Delta W\mu at every position, while the input is read and at every generated token, where μ\mu is the mean input of the matrix at the last token of held-out probes: held-out instructions given as bare prompts, disjoint from training. Removing the shared component keeps a⁡(x)−a¯=Δ​W​(z⁡(x)−μ)a(x)-\bar{a}=\Delta W(z(x)-\mu) at every position. The estimate of μ\mu does not depend on which probes or how many are used (Section D.8).

Across the 18 models (14 instruction-tuned and the 4 of Appendix C), the LoRA keeps 88%88\% [8383, 9292] of its gain on the traits and 92%92\% [8585, 9696] on the transformations with only its shared component, and 33%33\% [2323, 4343] and 57%57\% [4646, 6767] with it removed. These intervals resample models. Figure 15 draws every model, with the traits and the transformations apart.

The adaptation field of these LoRAs points along its shared component at a cosine of 0.840.84 [0.800.80, 0.870.87], and the shared component holds 71%71\% [6565, 7676] of the field’s energy, over the 18 models on the 9 behaviors. Both statistics are averaged over the layers the adapter reaches, as on the tasks (Section C.7). On behaviors as on tasks, the shared component alone keeps most of the gain, and removing it keeps far less.

D.6 Interventions on the maps

The cipher and the lookup are the two behaviors whose rule the model can only learn during adaptation. Over the 18 models, the LoRA keeps 84%84\% [7979, 8989] of its gain on the cipher and 64%64\% [5050, 7777] on the lookup with only its shared component, and 33%33\% [2020, 4646] and 19%19\% [99, 3030] with it removed. The lookup keeps the least of any benchmark, as expected for a table of new content (Section E.6), so part of the table sits in the LoRA’s input-specific component. A shift adapter trained directly on the lookup learns it (Section E.5).

D.7 Reading and writing

The interventions change what the adapter adds at every position. Here we ask at which positions the adapter has to be active at all. We keep the trained update unchanged in one phase and switch it off in the other. Active only while reading, the update is switched off at every generated position. Active only while writing, it is switched off while the input is read. Switching off acts on the same adapted matrices as the interventions. The first generated token comes from the forward pass over the input, so it belongs to the reading phase. We report each condition as a fraction of the run’s gain (Figure 16).

Across the 18 models, on the 6 generative behaviors and tasks (bullets, French, pirate, last word, conditional echo and GSM8K), over the 324324 runs, the update active only while reading keeps 83%83\% of the gain, and active only while writing 12%12\%. In a quarter of the 303303 runs whose gain reaches 0.050.05, reading alone keeps more than the full update, up to 165%165\%, so switching the adapter off during generation can raise adherence.

Two cases differ. On label-token classification, either phase alone suffices: the update at the last input position alone keeps 92%92\% to 101%101\% of the gain, and the update everywhere except that position keeps 68%68\% to 100%100\% (medians over the seeds of each of the 18 models, and 82%82\% reading and 99%99\% writing on DBpedia pooled, Figure 16). There is no generated text, and the update at the last position adds directly to the label logit. The order reverses on three behaviors of the base models: pirate on the base models behind Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B, where writing keeps 76%76\% and 81%81\% of the gain against −1%-1\% and 4%4\% for reading, and bullets on the Gemma-2-2B base model, where writing keeps 113%113\% against 41%41\%, every seed in the same order. In their saved generations the update active only while reading sets the first word and the model continues in its own register, and active only while writing the model starts in its own register and takes the persona or the list form within a sentence. Pirate on the Qwen2.5-7B base model leans the same way by a smaller margin (62%62\% against 47%47\%), with both phases producing the persona. On Gemma-2-2B with bullets the two phases tie (61%61\% against 56%56\%, the seeds split).

The shared component alone, in each phase. The test above switches the whole adapter on or off. We combine it with the first intervention to ask whether the shared component alone is enough within each phase. On 6 models (Llama-3.2-1B and 3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Gemma-2-2B), we apply only the shared component Δ​W​μ\Delta W\mu during one phase and nothing during the other, and compare it with the full adapter active in the same phase.

While the input is read, the shared component alone keeps a median 79%79\% of the gain over the 9090 generative runs whose gain reaches 0.050.05, against 92%92\% for the full adapter. The difference comes from one behavior on two models: pirate on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.2-1B, where the shared component keeps 37%37\% and 50%50\% against 69%69\% and 76%76\% for the full adapter. It does not come from pirate needing the input-specific component: applied in both phases, the same shared component keeps 89%89\% to 97%97\% on these models. In the saved generations, a run takes the persona in its first words or not at all.

While the answer is written, the shared component alone keeps as much of the gain as the full adapter in all 3030 medians over family and behavior, including Gemma-2-2B with bullets, where the two phases carry the same share (67%67\% against 66%66\%). On the transformations both keep 0%0\%. Wherever a phase carries part of the gain, the shared component alone carries the same part.

D.8 The estimate of the shared component and the evaluation size

The shared component is estimated from held-out probes. We check on 3 models from 3 families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B and SmolLM2-1.7B) that the number of probes does not move the fractions. The estimate converges quickly: its mean cosine to the estimate from all 200200 probes is 0.9880.988 from 1010 probes, 0.9950.995 from 2020 and 0.9990.999 from 100100. The fraction kept with only the shared component does not change with the number of probes: 94%94\% [9090, 9797] on the traits whether μ\mu comes from 2020, 4040 or 100100 probes (largest change 0.0010.001), and 95%95\% on the transformations. Most of the uncertainty comes from differences between runs: in adherence, the interval over runs for the drop on the traits, [0.0130.013, 0.0370.037], is wider than the bootstrap over probes within runs, [0.0210.021, 0.0280.028], so measurement noise within a run does not drive the pooled interval. Estimating μ\mu as the average input over every position of the prompt, instead of at its last token, keeps 55%55\% [4444, 6666] of the gain on the traits against 87%87\% [8282, 9292] at the last token, over the 18 models. The behavior relies on the component the adapter adds at the last token of the input.

D.9 The update without the rank constraint

LoRA factorizes its update into two low-rank matrices, so the shared component could be a product of that factorization. We therefore apply the two interventions to an update that is not factorized. We train the matrices that a rank-8 LoRA adapts directly, with the ordinary optimizer, and keep every other parameter frozen, so weight decay pulls the update toward zero and not toward the base weights. The update is WFT−W0W_{\mathrm{FT}}-W_{0}, and we intervene on it exactly as on LoRA’s, at every position of the input and the answer. The setup follows Section D.5, on the 18 models, the 4 traits and the 3 transformations. On the two maps, with only the shared component LoRA keeps 79%79\% [7070, 8787] of its gain and the unconstrained update 54%54\% [4646, 6161], and with it removed 26%26\% [1717, 3737] and 19%19\% [1010, 2929].

The update has high rank, and training without weight decay leaves its stable rank and the shared component’s share of the energy unchanged on the 18 models (47.847.8 and 97.2%97.2\%, against 46.646.6 and 97.2%97.2\% with it), so weight decay does not produce the high rank. Its shared component holds 95%95\% of the energy of what it adds (median 98%98\%), against 89%89\% for LoRA on the same runs (Section D.3), so the concentration does not come from the parameterization. The two methods gain about the same, a mean trait gain of 0.4420.442 for LoRA and 0.4370.437 without the rank constraint, so their fractions compare directly. Removing the whole update returns the model to the base model within 0.0200.020 in every run, so the interventions reach all of the update.
