On the 17 tasks, Mistral-7B has two routes to its gain: its LoRA keeps 75%75\% of the gain with only the shared component and 78%78\% with it removed, while for the largest instruction-tuned model of each other family, removing the shared component keeps 30%30\% to 76%76\%.

Without the rank constraint, the shared component holds more of the energy of the update and the behavior relies on it somewhat less, so the reliance does not come from the low rank.

D.10 In-context learning

In-context learning adapts without training, through demonstrations in the prompt. We apply the two interventions to the demonstrations and to a LoRA trained in the same runs, and call each of these two ways of adapting a route. A shift adapter trained in the same runs is a third route.

Experimental setup. We use the 18 models and the 9 behaviors of the setup: the traits French, bullet points, pirate and grumpy critic, the transformations copy, last word and conditional echo, and the maps cipher and lookup. In each run the demonstrations are four question–answer pairs before the query. For the traits, the answers are the model’s own answers under the behavior’s system prompt, each passing the behavior’s rule-based verifier, and the prompt uses the chat template. For the transformations and maps, the answers are the task’s targets, and the prompt is plain text behind a preamble that asks the model to continue the pattern, because an instruction-tuned model under its template answers the last question instead. The maps get their whole 2626-word table before the 4 examples, since 4 examples cover only 4 of its 2626 entries. The field of the demonstrations is the change they make to the hidden state at the last token of the input, h⁡(demonstrations+x)−h⁡(x)h(\text{demonstrations}+x)-h(x), and its shared component is the mean of that change over 4040 probe queries. To keep only the shared component, we add it to the bare query, one vector per layer at every position of the input and the answer, scaled by α∈{0.5,1,2}\alpha\in\{0.5,1,2\} chosen per family and class on seed 00. To remove it, we keep the demonstrations and subtract it at every position. As a control, a random vector of the same norm per layer is added and subtracted in the same way. A rank-8 LoRA and a shift adapter are trained in the same run on the same 160160 answers under the same prompt format, and the LoRA is run as trained, with only its shared component, and without it (Section D.1). Every route is scored on the same 4848 held-out queries, by the behavior’s rule-based verifier or, for pirate and grumpy critic, by token F1 against the model’s own answers under the system prompt. Fractions pool every run, and intervals resample models. The demonstration, probe, training and evaluation queries are disjoint.

Results. Figure 17 compares the two routes behavior by behavior. The demonstrations gain 0.300.30 on the traits, 0.600.60 on the transformations and 0.020.02 on the maps, where the LoRA gains 0.570.57, 0.940.94 and 0.870.87, and the shift adapter 0.570.57, 0.910.91 and 0.680.68. With only their shared component, the demonstrations keep 64%64\% [4747, 9292] of their gain on the traits and 46%46\% [4040, 5252] on the transformations, where the LoRA keeps 87%87\% [8282, 9191] and 89%89\% [8282, 9595]. On the maps the LoRA keeps 70%70\% [5959, 7979], and the demonstrations gain 0.020.02, too little for their fraction to mean anything (33%33\% [33, 8484]). Removing the shared component of the demonstrations keeps none of their gain: −25%-25\% [−43-43, −11-11] on the traits and −2%-2\% [−2-2, −1-1] on the transformations. Removing a random vector of the same norm keeps 15%15\% [−4-4, 3434] on the traits and 14%14\% [33, 2727] on the transformations, so on both the removal is specific to the shared component. Removing the shared component of the LoRA keeps 43%43\% [3131, 5555] on the traits and 62%62\% [5050, 7373] on the transformations.

Table 5 gives the values per model. Where the demonstrations gain little on the traits (0.000.00 on Qwen2.5-0.5B, 0.040.04 on Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-3B), the fraction is large and says little. Mistral-7B is the model whose LoRA keeps least of its gain on the transformations with only its shared component (35%35\%): in three of its 9 transformation runs, the shared component alone sends over 90%90\% of the answers into one repeated token.

Pirate and grumpy critic. On these two traits the score and the generations disagree. The demonstrations gain 0.110.11 on pirate and 0.050.05 on grumpy critic, and with only their shared component they fall below the base model on both (gains of −0.14-0.14 and −0.07-0.07), which lowers the pooled trait numbers above. We read the saved generations of 10 instruction-tuned models. Under the demonstrations, the generations of Mistral-7B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B carry a pirate marker as often as under the shift adapter (87%87\% to 99%99\% of them, against 98%98\% to 100%100\%), yet their F1 gain over the base model is 63%63\% to 106%106\% of the trained one (Mistral 0.420.42 against 0.410.41 for the shift adapter, SmolLM2 0.390.39 against 0.460.46), because the trained routes reproduce the teacher’s sentences and the demonstrations write their own. The three Qwen2.5 models carry the marker in 36%36\% to 41%41\% of their generations. Llama-3.2-1B refuses (“I can’t help with that”, F1 0.040.04 against 0.200.20 for the base model), and Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B continue the demonstration transcript (“I’ll answer your questions one by one, matey. Q: …”, markers in 49%49\% of their generations). The short pirate and grumpy critic spokes of Figure 17 therefore measure how closely the demonstrations reproduce the teacher’s answers, and the generations carry the pirate marker in 36%36\% to 99%99\% of cases in nine of these 10 models.

Shared components and fields through depth. Figure 18 compares the shared components of the three routes, and their fields, layer by layer. The shift adapter’s vector and the shared component of the demonstrations are orthogonal at every layer: the median cosine per layer decile lies between 0.000.00 and 0.030.03 on the traits and transformations and is at most 0.080.08 on the maps, and at most 0.310.31 in any run and layer. The shared component of the LoRA, the vector per layer that keeping only it adds, is also orthogonal to that of the demonstrations (median cosine per layer decile at most 0.040.04 on the traits and transformations and 0.090.09 on the maps, at most 0.300.30 in any run and layer). The two trained routes agree more with depth, from a median cosine of 0.150.15, 0.170.17 and 0.040.04 in the first layer decile on the traits, transformations and maps to 0.520.52, 0.680.68 and 0.840.84 in the last. The fields are not orthogonal. By the ninth layer decile, the fields of the shift adapter and the demonstrations reach a cosine of 0.470.47 on the traits and 0.510.51 on the transformations, the fields of the shared component of the LoRA and of the demonstrations 0.430.43 and 0.530.53, and the fields of the two trained routes 0.770.77 and 0.660.66, reaching 0.840.84 and 0.660.66 in the last decile. The trained routes add vectors orthogonal to the shared component of the demonstrations, and their fields meet the field of the demonstrations in the late layers.

On the tasks. We run the same two interventions on 4 of the tasks of Section 3, AG News, SST-2, OpenBookQA and HellaSwag, over the 18 models. Each run puts four label-balanced demonstrations before the query, takes their shared component as the mean change at the last token of the input over 300300 probe queries, and chooses the scale α∈{0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2\} on a held-out slice of 300300 rows. Every route is then scored on the task’s full evaluation split. A rank-8 LoRA trained in the same run on the task’s training rows, never on the demonstrations, is scored the same way.

Four demonstrations change these tasks little: the median gain over the runs is 0.0330.033 (quartiles 0.0110.011 to 0.0780.078), and one run (Llama-3.2-1B on AG News) ends 0.2670.267 below the bare prompt (Figure 19b). The demonstrations gain 0.050.05 or more on average only on AG News, SST-2 and OpenBookQA. With only their shared component, the demonstrations keep 42%42\% [2626, 5858] of their gain over every run, where the LoRA trained in the same runs keeps 83%83\% [7575, 8989] of its own, and a random vector of the same norm keeps −14%-14\% [−36-36, −1-1]. On AG News and SST-2 the demonstrations keep 50%50\% and 47%47\%, where the LoRA keeps 94%94\% and 96%96\% on the same runs (Figure 19a). On OpenBookQA the demonstrations keep 20%20\% where the LoRA keeps 78%78\%, and on HellaSwag their mean gain is below 0.050.05, too little for a fraction, while the LoRA keeps 66%66\%. The fractions of the LoRA on every task are in Section D.2. With 16 demonstrations, the shared component alone keeps 41%41\% [2323, 5858] and removing it keeps 49%49\% [3434, 6969], against 42%42\% and 39%39\% with four.

Removing the shared component from the prompt with the demonstrations keeps 39%39\% [1717, 5757], against 80%80\% [7171, 8787] for removing a random vector of the same norm, so the direction matters. The scale is chosen for keeping only the shared component and reused for the removal, and in 3535 of the 216216 runs the removal sends the model to one class, which widens the interval. At full strength it does so in every run, as on the behaviors. Through depth, the shared components of the two routes are orthogonal, with a median cosine per layer decile between 0.000.00 and 0.020.02 over all runs, while their fields converge, from 0.000.00 in the first decile to 0.740.74 in the last (quartiles [0.590.59, 0.850.85], Figure 19c). Table 6 gives the values per model. On behaviors and tasks, the shared component of the demonstrations is orthogonal to LoRA’s and keeps less of the gain than LoRA’s on the traits, the transformations and the tasks, so in-context learning reaches similar behaviors by a different route from LoRA.

Appendix E The shift adapter

E.1 The comparison on the tasks

We compare the shift adapter (Figure 20) with LoRAs of rank 11, 44, 88, 1616 and 6464. The shift adapter and the LoRAs are trained on the same teacher pairs, each at the learning rate selected for it (Section C.5), and every task is scored by accuracy on its whole labeled evaluation split. These splits are unbalanced, so the majority-class rate is reported beside every result.

Table 7 gives every task and every method, each with a bootstrap interval over the combinations of model and seed behind it, and the paired difference between the shift adapter and the rank-8 LoRA with its own interval. Pooled over the 18 models, the shift adapter reaches 0.7460.746 and the rank-8 LoRA 0.7450.745, against 0.6200.620 for the base model, a paired difference of +0.0006+0.0006 [−0.0007-0.0007, +0.0018+0.0018]. Against the other ranks the difference ranges from +0.0010+0.0010 [−0.0001-0.0001, +0.0021+0.0021] for rank 11 to −0.0022-0.0022 [−0.0034-0.0034, −0.0011-0.0011] for rank 6464. Per model it ranges from −0.006-0.006 on SmolLM2-1.7B to +0.011+0.011 on the base Gemma-2-2B, so no single model carries the result. Per task, the shift adapter leads on AQuA-RAT (+0.012+0.012), SuperGPQA (+0.008+0.008), SIQA (+0.007+0.007) and AG News (+0.005+0.005), and the LoRA leads most on HellaSwag (−0.008-0.008), MMLU-Pro (−0.007-0.007) and ARC-Challenge (−0.006-0.006). Figure 21 draws every task and every model. The selected learning rates of the shift adapter span a factor of 1,0001{,}000 across models and tasks, from 10−510^{-5} to 10−210^{-2}, against 5050 for the rank-8 LoRA, which is why each method trains at its own selected rate.

E.2 Full fine-tuning on the same tasks

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. We train it with AdamW in bfloat16 for 500500 steps, the budget of the LoRA, at a learning rate selected per model and task from the 6 rates of Section C.5, on the 17 tasks and 18 models, scored on the same evaluation splits. The shift adapter is retrained in the same run at its selected rate, so every difference is paired within a run. The retrained shift adapter reproduces the shift adapter of Table 7 to a mean absolute difference of 0.0040.004.

Pooled over the 18 models, full fine-tuning reaches 0.7180.718, the shift adapter and the rank-8 LoRA 0.7450.745, against 0.6200.620 for the base model, a paired difference between the shift adapter and full fine-tuning of +0.028+0.028 [+0.025+0.025, +0.030+0.030] (Table 8). The shift adapter is at or above full fine-tuning on every task except ARC-Challenge (−0.002-0.002), and leads most on WinoGrande (+0.066+0.066), CaseHOLD (+0.060+0.060) and HellaSwag (+0.057+0.057). Per model its lead ranges from +0.011+0.011 on Qwen3.6-27B to +0.069+0.069 on the base Gemma-2-2B. Over 900900 of these runs, the field of full fine-tuning has a cosine of 0.900.90 to its shared component and a field share of 0.810.81, against 0.910.91 and 0.830.83 for the rank-8 LoRA, paired differences of −0.009-0.009 and −0.015-0.015 (Figure 12c). Full fine-tuning moves every input in nearly the same direction, as LoRA does.

E.3 The comparison before instruction tuning

We repeat the comparison on the 3 models that never received instruction tuning (Section D.4), on the 17 tasks. The shift adapter reaches 0.7480.748 and the rank-8 LoRA 0.7430.743, against 0.5920.592 for the base model, a paired difference of +0.005+0.005 [+0.002+0.002, +0.008+0.008], and the shift adapter is at or above every rank from 11 to 6464. Full fine-tuning on the same models and tasks reaches 0.7070.707, below the shift adapter by +0.041+0.041 [+0.034+0.034, +0.048+0.048]. The parity with LoRA holds before instruction tuning, as the reliance on the shared component does (Section D.4).

E.4 The shift adapter and the LoRA push in the same direction

The shift adapter and the LoRA are trained independently on the same teacher pairs, so we ask whether they push the inputs in the same direction. On the 17 tasks and 18 models, with both trained in the same run, the shared component of the LoRA aligns with the shift adapter at a cosine of 0.640.64 [0.600.60, 0.680.68], against 0.060.06 [0.040.04, 0.080.08] for a rank-8 LoRA with random weights and no training, measured in the same runs. On the 9 behaviors and 18 models, the two align at 0.530.53 [0.500.50, 0.550.55], against 0.070.07 [0.050.05, 0.110.11] for the random LoRA (Figure 5). There, each input’s field points along its adapter’s shared component at a mean cosine of 0.850.85 [0.820.82, 0.870.87] for the shift adapter and 0.840.84 [0.800.80, 0.870.87] for the LoRA, against 0.660.66 [0.610.61, 0.710.71] for the random LoRA. Weighting each layer by how far the two adapters move it raises the agreement between the shift adapter and the LoRA to 0.690.69, while the random LoRA stays at 0.080.08 (Section C.7). A LoRA that can vary what it adds with every input pushes along the direction the shift adapter learns.

E.5 What a shift adapter can store

With only its shared component, LoRA keeps the least of its gain on the maps, whose rule the model can only learn during adaptation (Section D.6). A shift adapter trained directly on a map stores that content: it learns both maps, holds about 200200 entries of a table, and splits into a shared component that performs the lookup and stored content that holds the entries. A map separates capacity from content. The base model holds the capacity to look an entry up and answer with it, but the entries of the table are new content, which the shift adapter has to store. Trained on few items, a shift adapter therefore answers a map on the entries it saw and not on the others, as stored content predicts, while on the behaviors it reaches most of its gain on instructions never seen in training (Section E.6).

A shift adapter learns the maps. We train a shift adapter directly on the cipher and on a lookup table whose entries are assigned at random, on 5 models from 4 families, and score its held-out generations by exact match. Each map has seven possible answers, so we read the score against the majority-class rate, the score of always giving the most common answer. The shift adapter exceeds that rate on both maps in every family, by 0.080.08 to 0.380.38, with its answers spread over three to five of the seven, at the level of the LoRA. As a control, a third map, the number of words of the input modulo three, stays at or below the majority-class rate in every family. A shift adapter can therefore store content that pretraining never showed the model. The lower fraction on the maps in Section D.6 comes from the trained LoRA, which puts part of the map in its input-specific component, and a shift adapter trained directly on the map does without that component.

How much fits. We train a shift adapter on key–value tables of 100100 to 500500 entries and count the entries it answers on held-out queries. The count rises with the table, 9999, 146146, 181181, then 205205 at 250250 entries and 216216 at 300300, and then falls, to 185185 at 400400 entries and 115115 at 500500 (Figure 23). At 200200 entries the models answer 0.550.55 to 1.001.00 of the table. A shift adapter therefore holds about 200200 entries, and a larger table lowers the count. The field does not change at the limit: on the 5 families measured, from 100100 to 500500 entries, its magnitude (728728, 824824, 729729), the share of its energy in the shared component (0.430.43, 0.460.46, 0.450.45) and the effective rank of its input-specific component (5959, 5454, 5555) stay the same. Rank does not move the limit: a rank-1 LoRA holds 500 entries as well as a rank-64 one (0.9500.950 against 0.9490.949). With only its shared component, a trained LoRA keeps 14%14\% of its gain at 500 entries, against 76%76\% at 100100, so past the shift adapter’s limit the content sits in the LoRA’s input-specific component. Documents exceed the limit as well, and there the shift adapter stays close to the LoRA. On SQuAD a shift adapter recovers 56%56\% [5353, 5959] of the gain of reading the document in context, against 61%61\% [5959, 6464] for the LoRA, and on CoQA 13%13\% [1010, 1616] against 17%17\% [1414, 2121] (3030 held-out documents each, 5 families).

The shared component invokes the lookup, and the stored content supplies the entries. On the lookup, one trained shift adapter holds two things: the operation of looking an entry up, and the entries of one table. We separate them by construction. The shared component is estimated as the mean of 2424 shift adapters, each trained on a different table over one set of 5050 keys. With that estimate frozen in the model, a new per-layer vector, the stored content, is trained on the entries of a table outside the set. We then combine shared components and stored content from different sources and sort each generated answer into four kinds: the queried table’s entry, another table’s entry, an invented entry, and ordinary text (10 models, 4 tables of stored content, 4848 held-out prompts each). One generated answer for each combination is shown in Figure 22. The stored content alone leaves the model’s behavior unchanged. The shared component alone makes the model look an entry up with nothing to read, so it invents one (0.980.98 [0.970.97, 0.990.99] of answers). The shared component with another table’s stored content returns that table’s entries (0.990.99 [0.990.99, 1.001.00]). A shared component estimated from 2424 other tables still reads the stored content at 0.770.77 [0.700.70, 0.840.84], from 0.990.99 or more on every Llama model to 0.340.34 on SmolLM2-1.7B (Figure 24). Under a shared component trained for the reverse lookup, from value to key, the forward stored content returns 0.0000.000 [0.0000.000, 0.0010.001] of its entries, while a random direction at the same distance returns 0.760.76 [0.720.72, 0.810.81], so the stored content holds the table in the direction the forward lookup reads it. The shared component carries the operation, and the stored content carries the content it reads.

E.6 Training on few examples

In the experiments above, we saw that a shift adapter can store about 200200 table entries (Section E.5). One could therefore ask whether its success on the behaviors comes from simply storing its training examples, i.e., performing parameter-efficient memorization. To test this, we vary only the number of training examples. Across 4 architecture families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Gemma-2-2B) and 3 seeds, we train shift adapters and rank-8 LoRAs on 88, 3232 or 8080 training examples (88, 3232 or 160160 for the maps). For each seed, the training examples are drawn at random from the examples of the behavior. Every adapter is then evaluated on one set of 200200 held-out examples, none of which is ever used for training, so all scores are on examples the adapter has never seen. We report the fraction of the gain at the largest training size that is kept at each smaller size.

Behaviors. With 3232 training examples, a shift adapter keeps on average 83%83\% of its gain at 8080 training examples on the traits and 92%92\% on the transformations (Figure 25). With only 88 training examples, it keeps 59%59\% on the traits and 68%68\% on the transformations. A rank-8 LoRA trained on the same examples keeps 71%71\% and 66%66\%. The values per family are given in Table 9. All of these scores are on examples never seen in training, so the gain cannot come from storing the training examples. A few training examples thus suffice to actualize most of a behavior that the base model already holds.

Lookup tables. The maps are the opposite case. The base model has the capacity to look an entry up and answer with it, but the entries of a table are new content that it does not hold. The lookup maps the first letter of the input to one of 2626 unrelated words, so a correct answer can only come from a key seen in training. Trained on 88 training examples, which cover 88 of the 2626 keys, a shift adapter answers 28%28\% of the evaluation prompts whose key it saw, and 0.1%0.1\% of the prompts with one of the 1818 keys it never saw (Figure 26). A rank-8 LoRA behaves the same way (48%48\% and 0%0\%). The cipher, which substitutes letters, behaves the same way too: it answers 69%69\% on letters seen in training and none on the others, and its fraction in Figure 25c is high only because the 88 training examples start with the letters of most evaluation prompts. A shift adapter thus stores exactly the entries it was trained on, while on the behaviors it reaches most of its gain on examples it has never seen. This separates storing content from actualizing a capacity that the base model already holds.

Averaging over example sets. If a shift adapter stored its training examples, shift adapters trained on different examples would hold different content, and averaging them would cancel it. The three seeds of one behavior and family are trained on three disjoint sets of 88 training examples. We average their three shift adapters and evaluate the average on examples that none of the three was trained on, together with each single shift adapter in the same run. On the traits, the average keeps 59%59\% of the gain of the full-data shift adapter, compared to 47%47\% for a single one, and it is higher in each of the 4 families. A single shift adapter scaled to the norm of the average keeps 50%50\%, so the improvement comes from the direction the three share, not from a change of norm. Averaging shift adapters of different behaviors instead lowers the score below the base model. On the transformations, the average keeps as much as a single shift adapter (66%66\% and 65%65\%). On the lookup, where each seed saw different keys, it keeps less (7%7\% against 10%10\%).

Shift adapters trained on disjoint examples therefore find the same direction, and averaging them removes what is specific to each set of examples and strengthens the behavior. What a shift adapter learns from a few training examples is the direction that actualizes the behavior, not the examples themselves.

E.7 The shift adapter on the other tasks

The comparisons above evaluate each shift adapter on the task it is trained on. If a shift adapter improved the model in general, it would also raise the accuracy on the other tasks. We therefore evaluate every shift adapter on all 17 tasks, on the 18 models, and compare it to a random vector with the same norm at every layer. On its own task, the shift adapter raises accuracy by 0.1240.124 [0.1080.108, 0.1420.142] on average. On the 16 other tasks for which the shift adapter was not trained, accuracy changes by −0.004-0.004 [−0.011-0.011, +0.002+0.002] with the shift adapter and by −0.004-0.004 [−0.006-0.006, −0.001-0.001] with the random vector. The gain of a shift adapter is thus specific to the task it is trained on, and on average performance on other tasks remains at the base model’s accuracy.

Appendix F The structure of actualization

F.1 The principle at each checkpoint of OLMo-2-7B

To see when the two parts of the principle appear during training, we repeat the comparison of Section E.1 and the interventions of Section D.1 along the training of OLMo-2-7B, which AI2 publishes with more than 900900 intermediate checkpoints. We use 1515: five of stage-one pretraining on Dolma, at 11B, 99B, 105105B, 449449B and 3,8963{,}896B tokens, six of the 5050B-token stage two that follows, at 55B, 1313B, 2121B, 3030B, 3838B and 5050B tokens into it, from the first of the 3 stage-two runs whose average is the released base, and the released base, supervised, preference-tuned and instruct models. Each checkpoint follows the protocol of Section C.5 on the 17 tasks: for each task and method a rate is selected from six on a validation slice of the training split at seed 00, and every seed is trained on the whole training split at that rate and scored on the full evaluation split. The accuracy of the base model is the zero-shot accuracy of the checkpoint on the same split, read beside the split’s majority class. A run where neither method scores more than 0.020.02 above the majority class counts as a run in which the potentiality has not yet formed and stays in every average. The rank-8 LoRA of each run is then scored under the two interventions, with every run pooled and intervals clustered by task, since one checkpoint at 3 seeds has 1717 independent units, the tasks, and not 5151. Table 10 lists every checkpoint, Figure 6 draws it, and Figure 27 draws the task types with the LoRA beside the shift adapter.

By task type (Figure 27), the base model scores 0.570.57 on the three text classifications at 99B tokens and 0.820.82 at the released base, where the shift adapter reaches 0.860.86 and 0.960.96 and the LoRA 0.880.88 and 0.960.96. On the four commonsense question-answering tasks the base model rises from 0.420.42 at 11B tokens to 0.640.64 at the end of stage one and 0.700.70 at the released base, where the shift adapter and the LoRA both reach 0.810.81. On the three science question-answering tasks it stays at the majority class through 105105B tokens and reaches 0.530.53 at 449449B and 0.790.79 at the released base, where the shift adapter reaches 0.840.84 and the LoRA 0.860.86. On the four domain tasks it stays at the majority class through 105105B tokens and reaches 0.370.37 at 449449B and 0.500.50 at the released base, where the shift adapter reaches 0.520.52 and 0.620.62 and the LoRA 0.520.52 and 0.600.60. On HellaSwag it stays at the majority class through 105105B tokens and reaches 0.280.28 at 449449B, 0.440.44 at the released base and 0.520.52 at the instruct model, where the shift adapter reaches 0.710.71, 0.840.84 and 0.850.85 and the LoRA 0.750.75, 0.880.88 and 0.870.87. On the two expert question-answering tasks it stays at the majority class through 105105B tokens and reaches 0.140.14 at 449449B and 0.210.21 at the released base, where the shift adapter reaches 0.210.21 and 0.290.29 and the LoRA 0.210.21 and 0.300.30. From 449449B tokens on, the two adapters are within 0.040.04 of each other in every task type, and the LoRA leads clearly only at 11B tokens on the classifications, 0.480.48 against 0.360.36.

At the early checkpoints DBpedia, AG News and SST-2 are lifted above the majority class first, and the other tasks join as pretraining continues. At 11B tokens the LoRA lifts DBpedia to 0.510.51 and AG News to 0.410.41, where the shift adapter reaches 0.230.23 and 0.350.35 against majority classes of 0.070.07 and 0.250.25, and the LoRA alone lifts SST-2 slightly (0.530.53 against a majority class of 0.510.51). At 99B tokens the base model already scores 0.550.55 to 0.580.58 on these 3 tasks, and both methods lift them, DBpedia to 0.970.97, AG News to 0.880.88 and 0.870.87, and SST-2 to 0.740.74 and 0.810.81, while the other 14 tasks stay at the majority class. At 105105B tokens BoolQ, SIQA, SciQ and CaseHOLD join them. At 449449B tokens both methods lift every task but AQuA-RAT, and from 3,8963{,}896B tokens every task. Across all 255255 pairs of task and checkpoint, only three are lifted by one method alone: SST-2 at 11B and ARC-Easy at 105105B tokens by the LoRA (0.310.31 against 0.260.26, majority class 0.270.27), and CaseHOLD at 105105B tokens by the shift adapter (0.280.28 against 0.220.22, majority class 0.200.20).

With only the shared component, the LoRA keeps between 70%70\% and 93%93\% of its gain at every checkpoint, and with that component removed 4%4\% at 11B tokens, 25%25\% to 47%47\% over the rest of stage one and 51%51\% to 70%70\% from stage two on (Table 10). At every checkpoint the shared component alone keeps more of the gain than the rest of the update. At 11B and 99B tokens the LoRA gains little on most tasks, so both intervals are wide.

Figure 28 pools the 10 stage-two and released checkpoints per task. On every task, the two methods differ by at most 0.0240.024, the shift adapter’s lead on AQuA-RAT. The shift adapter trails the LoRA most on WinoGrande, ARC-Challenge and HellaSwag, by about 0.020.02 each, and by 0.0120.012 or less on the other tasks. On those 3 tasks the shared component of the LoRA keeps 76%76\%, 79%79\% and 89%89\% of its gain, and 67%67\% to 99%99\% on the other tasks with a gain. Over the 12 tasks with a fraction, the gap between the two methods and the fraction of the LoRA’s gain its shared component keeps correlate at Spearman +0.41+0.41 (p=0.19p=0.19).

F.2 Behaviors along the training of OLMo-2-7B

Beside the accuracy on the tasks, we count at each checkpoint how many of a fixed set of behaviors the model can be made to produce, by three routes: two demonstrations in the prompt, a trained shift adapter and a rank-8 LoRA, each adapter trained on 160160 questions and read on 4040 held-out ones.

Behaviors. Three classes of behavior can be scored without a teacher or a judgment. There are 4949 non-Latin writing systems, that is, answering in a language written in its own non-Latin script, such as Thai, Kannada, or Bengali, scored by Unicode script property, 4545 Latin-script languages, scored by a language identifier, and 4242 output forms, scored by the predicate each instruction states, such as answering only in questions or only in bullets. The output forms follow the verifiable-instruction construction of IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023). Several are its instruction types directly: no commas, a word or sentence count, bullets or a JSON object, capital letters, a forbidden word or letter, and a response language. The others, such as a sonnet or a pros-and-cons table, are built the same way. Every check refuses a degenerate answer, one that is too short, too repetitive or a phrase repeated in a loop, since such an answer can pass a predicate without following the instruction: a repeated character of a script passes a check that reads the share of letters in that script.

Criteria. A behavior is lifted when the adapter raises the model’s own rate on it by more than 0.050.05 over the 4040 held-out answers (Figure 29a, b), and reached when the model produces it in a majority of its answers, the criterion the prompt is held to and the one Figure 29c uses for both adapters.

Training target and learning rate. A pretraining checkpoint’s own answers under a system prompt do not contain the behavior: at 99B tokens they hold the requested script in 00 of 4949 writing systems. We therefore train every checkpoint toward the instruct model’s answers to the same 160160 questions, one target for every checkpoint, and score every answer against the instruction itself. That target produces 4242 of the 4949 writing systems, 3838 of the 4545 languages and 2020 of the output forms, and those are the counts below. The learning rate is selected per checkpoint, class and method, from 4 rates for the shift adapter and 3 for the LoRA, with a higher rate added wherever the highest one won, as the rate that reaches the most behaviors at seed 00, and every seed is read at it (Section F.4).

Results. At 11B tokens OLMo-2-7B produces none of the 4242 writing systems by any route. At 99B tokens two demonstrations reach 1616 of them, a rank-8 LoRA 4040 to 4141 across the seeds, and a trained shift adapter 55 to 66. From 105105B tokens on, the three routes stay close to the whole set: the prompt between 3030 and 4141, the shift adapter between 3333 and 4242, and the LoRA between 4040 and 4242 at every later checkpoint (Figure 29c). At 7 further checkpoints between 99B and 105105B tokens, a trained shift adapter reaches 66, 1010, 2222, 2121, 2929, 3030, 3232, 3939 and 4141 of the 4242 writing systems at 99B, 1313B, 2121B, 3030B, 4242B, 5555B, 6868B, 8484B and 105105B tokens, while a rank-8 LoRA stays between 3636 and 4242. A rank-8 LoRA reaches these writing systems at 99B tokens only with both of its components, while the shared component that a shift adapter actualizes forms between 99B and 105105B tokens, as the shift adapter reaches more of them (Section F.11). The other two classes follow the same order. On the 3838 languages the prompt reaches 33 at 99B tokens, the shift adapter 00 to 11 and the LoRA 3131 to 3434, and at 105105B tokens the three reach 1111, 1616 to 2626 and 3535 to 3737. On the 2020 output forms the LoRA reaches 1212 to 1313 at 99B tokens, against 33 to 44 for the shift adapter and 55 for the prompt, and from 105105B tokens on all three sit between 88 and 1515. Over all 100100 behaviors the LoRA reaches 8484 at 99B tokens, the shift adapter 99 to 1111 and the prompt 2424, and at the instruct model the three reach 9090 to 9191, 8888 to 9393 and 8282 (Figure 29b). The distance between the LoRA and the shift adapter is widest at the earliest checkpoints and closes as pretraining continues.

The prompt along the training. Over all 100100 behaviors the prompt falls from 9191 at the supervised model to 8282 after preference tuning and at the instruct model. Open-Assistant’s supervised chain from Pythia-12B shows the same fall, from 3737 of the 4040 writing systems at the base model to 2929. In both post-training chains the instruction-tuned model follows a bare sequence of demonstrations less closely than the base model it came from, while both adapters reach the same behaviors. From 105105B tokens on, the share of the prompt’s behaviors that a shift adapter reaches does not depend on how strongly the prompt reaches them: it is within 1313 points whether the prompt reaches a behavior in all eight of its answers or in fewer (AUC 0.300.30 to 0.560.56, permutation p≥0.352p\geq 0.352). At 99B tokens, the few behaviors a shift adapter reaches are those the prompt reaches best, 55 of 55 against 1616 of 2323 (AUC 0.760.76, p=0.023p=0.023).

F.3 Two further models: OLMo-2-1B and Pythia-12B

OLMo-2-1B, a second model with two pretraining stages, repeats the measurement at 1212 checkpoints with the same target and the same rate rule (Figure 30a). At 11B tokens a rank-8 LoRA already reaches 3838 to 3939 of the 4242 writing systems, where two demonstrations reach none and a trained shift adapter 00 to 22. At 2121B tokens the prompt reaches 2626 and the shift adapter 1818 to 2121, and from 105105B tokens on the three routes stay between 2828 and 4242, reaching 3838, 4141 to 4242 and 4141 to 4242 at the released base model. Pythia-12B, trained on the Pile by EleutherAI without a second pretraining stage, has no instruct model of its own, so its adapters train toward the answers of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to the same questions. A rank-8 LoRA reaches 3939 to 4040 of the 4040 writing systems that target produces at every one of its 88 checkpoints, including the first at 2.12.1B tokens, where the prompt and a trained shift adapter reach none (Figure 30b). A trained shift adapter reaches 44 to 88 at 6.36.3B tokens, 1919 to 2222 at 16.816.8B, 3030 to 3434 at 54.554.5B and 3232 to 3939 from 170170B tokens on, against 2424 to 3737 for the prompt over the same range. In all 3 models a rank-8 LoRA reaches these behaviors at the first checkpoint we measure, and a shift adapter reaches them later, in Pythia-12B after about 5050 times more tokens. A constant thus actualizes a behavior once pretraining has formed the capacity for it, as the principle predicts, while a LoRA can reach it earlier by adding what the base model lacks (Section F.11).

F.4 The learning rate along the training

The selected rate varies along the training and between the classes of behavior. Over the 9292 runs of a checkpoint and a class, the shift adapter takes 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} in 6666, 10−310^{-3} in 1313, 10−210^{-2} in 1212 and 3×10−23\times 10^{-2} in 11, and the rank-8 LoRA 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} in 5151, 6×10−46\times 10^{-4} in 2828, 6×10−56\times 10^{-5} in 1212 and 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} in 11. Wherever the highest rate of the range wins, a higher rate is also trained and loses. The separation at 99B tokens does not depend on the selection: no rate of the shift adapter reaches more than 66 writing systems there, while the LoRA reaches 3939 to 4141 at three of its rates.

F.5 What a shift adapter reaches early is new text

A behavior a shift adapter reaches early could be text the checkpoint has seen and repeats. We count exact nn-grams of the shift adapter’s own generations for the writing systems in the Dolma corpus (Soldaini et al., 2024) that OLMo-2 was trained on, through the infini-gram index (Liu et al., 2024a). The share found falls with length, 58%58\% of bigrams, 11%11\% of 55-grams and 5%5\% of 1010-grams, which shows that the index finds text where it exists. A behavior’s corpus overlap and the checkpoint at which its shift adapter first reaches it correlate at ρ=0.03\rho=0.03 over 9999 behaviors (Figure 31). A shift adapter that reaches a behavior early makes the model write new text in it.

F.6 Width of the region in magnitude and direction

We train a shift adapter for each of the setup’s 4 traits on the 18 models, and vary its magnitude and its angle to the trained direction, scoring 256256 held-out probes at every point. Each pair of model and trait trains at its own rate, since the rate that maximizes trained adherence spans a factor of 4040 across the 18 models and varies as widely between the traits of one model. We select it from 5 rates between 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} and 2×10−32\times 10^{-3}, as the rate with the highest trained adherence, with ties going to the smaller rate.

Pooled adherence is 0.0150.015 [0.0120.012, 0.0190.019] at 0.25×0.25\times the trained magnitude, 0.0770.077 [0.0580.058, 0.0970.097] at 0.5×0.5\times, 0.4340.434 [0.3950.395, 0.4750.475] at the trained magnitude, 0.1400.140 [0.0940.094, 0.1840.184] at 2×2\times, and −0.011-0.011 [−0.050-0.050, 0.0300.030] at 4×4\times, and a 90∘90^{\circ} rotation leaves −0.005-0.005 [−0.009-0.009, −0.001-0.001] (Figure 32a). Rotated by 45∘45^{\circ}, the shift adapter keeps more at twice the trained magnitude (0.2480.248) than at the trained magnitude (0.2310.231): at twice the magnitude its component along the trained direction is 1.411.41 times the trained one, the component that sets the edge (Section F.7). At twice the trained magnitude, bullets keep 58%58\% of their peak and French 35%35\%, while pirate and grumpy critic fall below the base model (−19%-19\% and −38%-38\%, Figure 32b). The peak reproduces across the seeds of a pair: the standard deviation of its adherence over the seeds has a median of 0.0110.011 and is at most 0.0850.085 over the pairs.

Distance from the base model’s states. We also measure how far the adapted state at the last input token lies from the base model’s, on 6464 held-out prompts over the second half of the layers: the median over prompts of the mean distance to the 88 nearest base states, divided by the same distance among the base states, so that 11 is as close as the base states lie to each other. The distance rises with magnitude, from 0.910.91 at 0.25×0.25\times and 1.041.04 at 0.5×0.5\times to 1.471.47 [1.421.42, 1.511.51] at the trained magnitude, 1.791.79 at 2×2\times and 2.342.34 at 4×4\times. Rotated by 90∘90^{\circ} at the trained magnitude, the state lies at 0.980.98 [0.950.95, 1.001.00]. Below half the trained magnitude, the state stays among the base model’s states and the behavior is not produced. Above the trained magnitude, the state moves further from them while adherence falls.

F.7 Where the edge of the region falls

To locate the edge, we measure the 18 models and the setup’s 4 traits at 9 angles and 7 magnitudes near the trained scale. Adherence halves 44.1∘44.1^{\circ} from the trained direction. An edge is read per run as the point where the straight line between two neighboring grid points crosses the threshold, and we report the median over runs. On the 4 traits of the setup, on the 18 models, the edge at 90%90\% of the trained shift adapter’s gain runs from 0.830.83 to 1.251.25 times the trained magnitude and to 31.4∘31.4^{\circ}, and the edge at half the gain from 0.700.70 to 1.661.66 times and to 44.1∘44.1^{\circ}. The same grid on the 12 verifiable instruction types of IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023), on the 18 models, puts the edge at 90%90\% of the gain from 0.920.92 to 1.051.05 times the trained magnitude and at 16.4∘16.4^{\circ}, and the edge at half the gain from 0.590.59 to 1.271.27 times and at 58.7∘58.7^{\circ}. There a program decides compliance with no teacher, and the shape is the same: a narrow band in magnitude and a wide one in direction. On the 5 rule behaviors of the setup, on the 18 models, the edge at 90%90\% of the gain runs from 0.700.70 to 1.401.40 times the trained magnitude and to 42.6∘42.6^{\circ}, and the edge at half the gain spans the whole measured range of magnitudes, 0.50.5 to 22 times, and reaches 58.1∘58.1^{\circ}. Per behavior the half-gain angle runs from 52.1∘52.1^{\circ} (lookup) to 67.5∘67.5^{\circ} (copy), wider than on any trait. The per-trait medians span 39.8∘39.8^{\circ} (grumpy critic) to 47.2∘47.2^{\circ} (bullets). A magnitude above the trained one costs less than one below it: the median pair keeps 0.0700.070 more of its peak at 1.5×1.5\times than at 0.7×0.7\times (mean 0.0610.061), and 44 of the 71 pairs of model and trait favor 1.5×1.5\times.

Write a perturbed state in the coordinates the perturbation itself uses, a component α​cos⁡θ\alpha\cos\theta along the trained direction and a component α​sin⁡θ\alpha\sin\theta across it. The second is exact, since the perturbation orthogonalizes the added direction against the trained one before rotating. The first alone sets the edge. One shared curve in α​cos⁡θ\alpha\cos\theta accounts for a median 0.6170.617 of the variation within one run, against 0.2390.239 for the distance from the trained state, 0.2610.261 for the angle and 0.1310.131 for the magnitude. On the traits, the band of α​cos⁡θ\alpha\cos\theta that holds half the peak runs from 0.700.70 to 1.661.66 (0.600.60 to 1.841.84 with the rule behaviors), and inside that band the fall-off changes by at most 0.160.16 of the peak as the across component grows to twice the trained norm (0.280.28 at any fixed α​cos⁡θ\alpha\cos\theta). The angle at which adherence halves therefore climbs with magnitude, from 33.9∘33.9^{\circ} at 0.85×0.85\times to 44.1∘44.1^{\circ} at the trained magnitude and 70.0∘70.0^{\circ} at 2×2\times over the runs that still fall below half there, which is what a constant α​cos⁡θ\alpha\cos\theta predicts. A region is therefore a band in that one component: what a state keeps depends on how much of the trained direction it retains.

F.8 What the shift adapter is rotated toward

We measure how far the edge depends on the kind of direction the shift adapter is rotated toward. The magnitude is held at the trained one and the added direction is drawn three ways: at random, inside the span of the other traits’ shift adapters, and along another trait’s own shift adapter. On the 4 traits of the setup and the 18 models, the shift adapter keeps 90%90\% of its gain up to 31.3∘31.3^{\circ} toward a random direction, 23.8∘23.8^{\circ} toward a direction inside the span and 12.9∘12.9^{\circ} toward another trait’s shift adapter, and half of it up to 43.9∘43.9^{\circ}, 38.6∘38.6^{\circ} and 25.6∘25.6^{\circ}. On the 5 rule behaviors, turning toward another behavior’s state halves the gain at 36.0∘36.0^{\circ} and keeps 90%90\% up to 22.0∘22.0^{\circ}, against 58.1∘58.1^{\circ} and 42.6∘42.6^{\circ} toward a random direction (Section F.7). A region is about twice as wide across the directions the model does not use for another trait as across the directions it does, and the random edge exceeds the other-trait edge in 205205 of the 213213 runs and in all 4 traits. The in-span edge sits below the random edge in every trait. On the traits of the setup, the random edge agrees with that of Section F.7, 43.9∘43.9^{\circ} against 44.1∘44.1^{\circ}, on separate runs (Figure 33).

F.9 Connectivity of the region

We score adherence along the straight segment between two states of one behavior trained at different seeds, on the 18 models. The test is sketched in Figure 34. We summarize each path by its lowest interior point, as a share of the mean adherence of its two endpoints. The path stays adherent along its whole length: over 369369 segments on 10 traits, the lowest interior point keeps a median 100%100\% of the endpoint gain (100%100\% on bullets and French, 156156 segments, and 96%96\% on one word, the lowest trait), and the worst per-model mean barrier, over the segments scored at two evaluation seeds, is −0.019-0.019 (Mistral-7B), at endpoint cosines from 0.130.13 on Tulu-3-8B-SFT to 0.910.91 on Gemma-2-2B (Figure 35). On the 5 rule behaviors of the setup, on the 18 models, the lowest interior point on the line between two trained states keeps a median 98%98\% of their gain, from 90%90\% on the cipher and 94%94\% on the lookup to 100%100\% on copy, while the same line toward a random direction of the same norm keeps 0%0\%. Two states that share a sixth of their direction still connect without a trough, so the states that produce one behavior form one connected region. The two states need not share their supervision. A state trained on external gold answers (the base model’s own answers translated by a separate machine-translation model) and one distilled from a system prompt stay connected in all 11 models, and this holds in each of 3 languages: the lowest interior point keeps a median 98%98\% of the endpoint gain in French and German and 100%100\% in Spanish, never below 86%86\%, with the target language above 0.870.87 at every midpoint, 3333 of 3333 model–language pairs. Both routes reach the language they were trained for, so no path is scored on a state that never produced it (lowest rate over the 3333 runs per language 0.920.92, 0.880.88 and 0.880.88, medians 1.001.00, 1.001.00 and 0.960.96). A random direction of the same norm connects in none of the 3333. The two states connect whether or not a nearest-neighbor ranking of their fields places them close: in French the gold state is the prompt state’s nearest neighbor in 66 of the 1111 models and 22nd to 1818th in 44, and it connects even on Qwen2.5-0.5B, where the ranking puts it 249249th among the model’s trait states (1313th to 2020th in German).

F.10 Region size and the strength of the behavior

On the setup. For each pair of model and behavior, we take the area of the region of actualizing states, the share of the magnitude-by-angle grid of Section F.7 on which a perturbed shift adapter keeps half the trained gain, and the adherence of the trained state, each as the mean over runs. The pairs are the 4 traits and 5 rule behaviors of the setup on the 18 models. A larger region gives a stronger behavior (Figure 36). Within a model, the area correlates with the adherence at Spearman +0.64+0.64 on average (median +0.68+0.68) over the 18 models, and the correlation is positive in every one of them, from +0.13+0.13 on Qwen2.5-0.5B to +0.87+0.87 on Llama-3.2-3B. Over all pairs it is +0.68+0.68 (p<10−22p<10^{-22}).

What a region looks like. Figure 37 shows the plane through 4 independently trained states of one behavior, for 5 behaviors on the 18 models. French, pirate and excited child occupy bounded regions whose size differs across models, while bullets and one word fill the whole measured plane, so their regions exceed the window and their reported area is a lower bound. The mean area over the 5 behaviors runs from 0.480.48 on SmolLM2-1.7B to 0.840.84 on Qwen2.5-7B.

Along training. At each of 6 stages of OLMo-2-7B, we measure the region on the plane through 3 independently trained states of each of 10 behaviors that a shift adapter reaches by 449449B tokens, as the share of the plane whose adherence stays at or above half its peak. The area rises from 0.130.13 at 449449B tokens and 0.170.17 at the end of stage one to 0.400.40 at the released base and 0.780.78, 0.800.80 and 0.790.79 after supervised, preference and instruction tuning (Figure 38). Across these 6060 planes, the area predicts the peak adherence on the plane at Spearman +0.84+0.84, with a positive correlation within every stage.

F.11 When the shared component forms during pretraining

In the sections above, we showed that a rank-8 LoRA produces nearly every writing system (answering in a language written in its own non-Latin script) from the early checkpoints of OLMo-2-7B on, while a shift adapter produces them from 105105B tokens on (Section F.1). This leaves two possibilities. A constant that produces the writing systems may already exist at 99B tokens, and training a shift adapter from zero may not find it. Or no such constant exists yet, and the LoRA reaches the writing systems in another way. We can use the interventions defined in Section D.1 to distinguish the two, since they test whether the gain of the trained LoRA depends on its shared component.

Setup. We train on OLMo-2-7B at the checkpoints of 99B and 105105B tokens, with the protocol of Section F.1 and 3 seeds. A writing system counts as produced when it appears in the majority of 4040 held-out answers, and we count over the 4242 writing systems of Section F.1. We train every method anew at 3 seeds, so the counts differ by a few from Figure 29. We compare the following states:

  • •

    A rank-8 LoRA, evaluated in full, with only its shared component, and with its shared component removed. These interventions tell whether the gain of the trained LoRA rests on a constant.

  • •

    A shift adapter trained from zero, as in Section F.1.

  • •

    A shift adapter started from the demonstrations. Its training starts from the shared component of two demonstrations of the target (Section D.10) instead of from zero. If a suitable constant existed near the one the demonstrations give, training from there would find it more easily.

  • •

    The demonstrations, given in the prompt, and their shared component added on its own.

  • •

    A random vector with the same norm as the shift adapter at every layer. It shows that a vector of this size does not produce the writing systems by itself.

At 99B tokens. The full LoRA produces 4040 to 4242 of the 4242 writing systems (Table 11). Its shared component alone produces none of them in any seed, and at most one at any learning rate we tried. Removing the shared component also leaves none. At this checkpoint, the LoRA thus reaches the writing systems only through both of its components together, and no part of its gain comes from a constant. The other constants agree: the shift adapter started from the demonstrations produces at most two, and the shared component of the demonstrations added on its own and the random vector produce none. Trained from zero, the shift adapter reaches 77 to 88.

At 105105B tokens. The shared component of the LoRA alone now produces 3737 to 4040 writing systems, while removing it leaves none: the gain of the LoRA now rests entirely on its shared component. A shift adapter trained from zero produces 3838 to 4141, nearly as many as the full LoRA (4242), and one started from the demonstrations 2424 to 3333 (Figure 39). The random vector still produces none.

The two checkpoints thus show when the capacity forms. At 99B tokens, a LoRA already produces the writing systems, but not through a constant: neither its own shared component nor any other constant we tested produces them. At 105105B tokens, the LoRA’s own shared component produces almost all of them, and a shift adapter trained from zero finds a constant that does the same. The capacity that a constant can actualize therefore forms during pretraining, between 99B and 105105B tokens. We measure this on the trained LoRA itself, through its interventions, so the result does not depend on whether training a shift adapter succeeds. The potentiality and actuality principle thus states not only how adaptation works, but also from which point in pretraining it applies.

F.12 Predicting before adaptation whether an actualizing state exists

The potentiality and actuality principle says that a shift adapter actualizes a capacity that the base model already holds. If so, it should be possible to see in the base model, before any adapter is trained, whether an actualizing state exists for a task. We test this with a linear readout of the hidden states of the unadapted model.

Setup. We use 66 rules that map a list of 11 to 1212 pseudo-words to one of 33 answers: the word count modulo 33, the word count mapped to the 33 answers by a fixed random table, the first letter mapped by such a table, the letter count and the vowel count modulo 33, and random labels, which follow no rule. On 4 architecture families, we train a shift adapter on 10,00010{,}000 inputs for each rule (300300 or 1,0001{,}000 for the random labels) and evaluate it on held-out inputs, whose words never appear in training. Separately, before any adaptation, we fit a linear readout that predicts the answer from the hidden states of the unadapted model. The readout is fit at every input position and at 6 depths, and its position and depth are chosen on validation inputs. A rule can sit at different positions: the first letter, for instance, is read without error at the first token of the input, but at only 0.120.12 to 0.300.30 at the last token.

Results. For every rule that a shift adapter learns, the readout of the base model already recovers the answer (Table 12). On the first letter, the word count, and the relabelled length, the shift adapter reaches 0.700.70 to 1.001.00 on held-out inputs, and the readout 0.770.77 to 1.001.00. On the letter count, the vowel count, and the random labels, the readout stays near chance, and so does the shift adapter, as the principle predicts (0.310.31 to 0.400.40, with chance at 0.330.33). Across all 2424 pairs of rule and model, no shift adapter learns a rule that the readout of the base model does not already recover (Figure 40). Across the 2424 pairs, the accuracy of the shift adapter follows that of the readout, at a Pearson correlation of 0.980.98 and a Spearman correlation of 0.840.84.

Where adaptation has to add. The readout also indicates in advance where an actualizing state does not exist, and adaptation has to add to the base model. On the vowel count, which the readout does not recover, a rank-8 LoRA reaches 0.430.43 and 0.480.48 on Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, and a rank-64 LoRA 0.550.55 and 0.520.52, while the shift adapter stays near chance, at 0.370.37 and 0.360.36. A LoRA can add what the base model lacks, while a constant, as the principle predicts, actualizes only what the base model holds.

A shift adapter thus actualizes what the base model already represents, and whether an actualizing state exists can be estimated on the base model before adaptation. Together with Section F.11, this suggests a condition for the potentiality and actuality principle: a capacity can be actualized once the base model represents what the task needs, and the base model comes to represent it during pretraining.

Appendix G Implications

G.1 Steering: extraction against training

Steering adds a vector to the hidden states of the model. We compare vectors extracted without training with the shift adapter trained on the same behavior, on the 9 behaviors of the setup and the 18 models.

Experimental setup. Three extraction methods give one steering vector per behavior: the mean difference of CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024), the leading principal component of the same differences (Zou et al., 2023), and the in-context task vector (Hendel et al., 2023). Each is added at the single best layer or at every layer, 6 variants in all, each added the way the shift adapter adds its vectors, one vector per layer. An extracted vector gives a direction but not a strength, so the strength of each variant is chosen from 5 values on 200200 held-out instructions, and every method is scored on 800800 further held-out instructions. The shift adapter trains on 400400 instructions for 200200 steps. For each run, the best extracted direction is the variant with the highest adherence on the 800800 instructions, a choice that favors extraction. Scores follow Section C.6: adherence on the traits, where 00 is the base model, and the exact-match rate on the transformations and maps.

Results. Pooled over the 9 behaviors, the trained shift adapter reaches a score of 0.680.68 [0.620.62, 0.720.72], against 0.170.17 [0.140.14, 0.200.20] for the best extracted direction (Table 13). Per class, the shift adapter reaches 0.450.45 on the traits against 0.200.20, 0.870.87 on the transformations against 0.100.10, and 0.830.83 on the maps against 0.230.23. The extracted directions come close to the trained shift adapter only on bullet points (0.880.88 against 0.890.89), and stay at or below the base model on French, pirate and grumpy critic, where the shift adapter reaches 0.190.19 to 0.430.43. On the transformations and maps, the best extracted direction reaches at most 0.430.43, on the cipher, against 0.780.78 to 0.990.99 for the shift adapter.

G.2 Steering on AxBench

AxBench (Wu et al., 2025) steers on 500500 concepts drawn from a sparse autoencoder of Gemma-2, each a text description with positive and negative examples. We train a shift adapter and a rank-8 LoRA on Gemma-2-2B for every concept, 6 rates for the shift adapter and 4 for the LoRA, and score them on the two axes of the benchmark. Steering is judged by GPT-4o-mini, the benchmark’s judge model, on each generation with its prompts unchanged: the presence of the concept, the relevance to the instruction and the fluency, each from 00 to 22, combined by their harmonic mean. Detection is the concept-against-negative separation the trained state gives when read as a probe. Each method’s rate is the one with the best steering score, chosen for every concept on the other 499499 concepts, so that a concept never takes part in choosing its own rate. This gives 3×10−23\times 10^{-2} for the shift adapter and 6×10−46\times 10^{-4} for the LoRA on every concept, and both ranges continue past these rates. Each concept is judged on its own held-out instructions at 6464 generated tokens, where the benchmark’s leaderboard judges 1010 fixed instructions at 128128 tokens, so our levels are not its leaderboard numbers and the comparison is between the two methods under one protocol. On the benchmark’s steering score the shift adapter reaches 0.8670.867 and the LoRA 0.9140.914, a paired difference of −0.047-0.047 [−0.072,−0.021][-0.072,-0.021] over the 500500 concepts, −0.05-0.05, −0.06-0.06 and −0.04-0.04 on the seeds (Figure 41b). On adherence to the reference answer, the score of the main text, the shift adapter reaches 0.0640.064 against 0.0730.073 for the LoRA, a paired difference of −0.009-0.009 [−0.011,−0.007][-0.011,-0.007] (Figure 41a). At the rate the judge selects, the shift adapter puts the concept into more of its answers and keeps less of the reference wording, and at 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} its adherence is 0.0900.090, above the LoRA’s. On the presence of the concept alone the shift adapter scores 0.9650.965 and the LoRA 0.9830.983, and on the other two judged scores it is below the LoRA, by 0.090.09 on relevance to the instruction and by 0.020.02 on fluency. On detection the shift adapter reaches an area under the curve of 0.5710.571, above chance on 374374 of the 500500 concepts, and the LoRA 0.6860.686, above chance on 464464, a difference of −0.115-0.115 [−0.126,−0.105][-0.126,-0.105] (Figure 41c). The rate moves the three scores apart: from 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} to 3×10−23\times 10^{-2} the steering score rises from 0.8510.851 to 0.8670.867, while adherence falls from 0.0900.090 to 0.0640.064 and the area under the curve from 0.6070.607 to 0.5710.571. A shift adapter steers within 6%6\% of the LoRA, and the state of the LoRA separates the concept from its negatives better.

Programming and the web make up 20%20\% of the concepts and science 7%7\%, and none of the 500500 is one of our behaviors: none is a writing system, a language or an output form, and the one that names a language we test names it as a topic. The parity of Section 3 therefore holds across two concept sets that do not intersect.

Extracted directions on the same protocol. We compare the trained methods with 3 directions extracted without training, as in Section 5, on the same concepts and under the same protocol. The mean difference is, at every decoder block, the mean hidden state over the response tokens of the concept’s 4848 training examples minus the mean over those of the 6464 shared negatives, AxBench’s DiffMean and the contrast of CAA. The principal component is the leading component of the same positives centered on the negative mean, sign-aligned with the mean difference (Zou et al., 2023). The in-context direction is the last-token displacement that a prompt of 4 of the concept’s examples induces over the bare prompt, averaged over 1616 of its instructions (Hendel et al., 2023). Each direction is added the way the shift adapter adds its vectors, one vector per block, the unit direction at a block scaled by a multiple of the base model’s activation norm there, at every block or, for the mean difference, at AxBench’s block 2020 alone. The multiples bracket the best value (0.0050.005 to 0.080.08 at every block, 0.020.02 to 0.80.8 at one block), the multiple of each direction is the smallest one within 0.0050.005 of the best steering score, chosen for every concept on the other 499499 concepts, the rule that selects the trained methods’ rates, and each direction is judged on the same two held-out instructions per concept as the trained methods. Table 14 gives the result. The best extracted direction, the mean difference at every block, reaches a steering score of 0.2070.207 at multiple 0.040.04 and 0.0170.017 at 0.080.08, where the generations degenerate. At block 2020 it reaches 0.1800.180, the principal component 0.1600.160 and the in-context direction 0.1660.166. The trained shift adapter reaches 0.8670.867 and the LoRA 0.9140.914 on the same concepts, a paired difference of −0.660-0.660 [−0.697,−0.623][-0.697,-0.623] between the best extracted direction and the shift adapter. On the concept sub-score the extracted directions reach 0.160.16 to 0.260.26 against 0.970.97 for the shift adapter, and they raise the steering score above zero on 7676 to 132132 of the 500500 concepts against 435435 for the shift adapter and 446446 for the LoRA. Their relevance sub-scores are above those of the trained methods, and so is their fluency, except for the mean difference at every block (0.790.79). The level of the mean difference at block 2020, 0.1800.180, is the level the benchmark’s own board reports for it, 0.1780.178 (Wu et al., 2025), under a protocol that differs in the instructions and the length judged.

G.3 Convergence across models

Conventions. The permutation test of each of the 9191 pairs in Section 5 is a pairwise comparison and carries no family-wise correction. Every comparison of the 14 atlases uses the 7575 behaviors that every atlas holds (Section C.4). The association with capability is unchanged (ρ=0.68\rho=0.68) when capability is measured in bits per byte instead of log-likelihood per token. RSA and mutual-kkNN rise with the capability of the pair and CKA does not (Figure 42): over the 9191 pairs, RSA at Spearman ρ=0.68\rho=0.68 (p=0.003p=0.003), mutual-kkNN at ρ=0.40\rho=0.40 (p=0.033p=0.033) and CKA at ρ=−0.38\rho=-0.38 (p=0.93p=0.93), each pp from a one-sided permutation of the model labels. The 3 measures differ in what they cannot see. RSA ranks the cosines between states, so it does not see one state rescaled or the cosines changed in any order-preserving way. CKA centers the atlas first, so it does not see the atlas moved as a whole or rescaled. Mutual-kkNN reads neighbor sets, so it does not see any change that leaves each state’s neighbors in place. A rotation of the coordinates is invisible to all three: a similarity between two atlases reads the pattern of distances among their states, not their coordinates, which differ from model to model. Figure 43 draws the similarity over the 9191 pairs and through depth.

G.4 Neural thickets

Gan and Isola (2026) add Gaussian noise of a fixed size to every weight of a pretrained model, score each perturbed model on a selection split, and keep the best, which they call experts. Under the principle, a perturbation finds an expert only where the region of actualizing states of the behavior is wide enough to be hit by chance (Section 5). We repeat their search on the setup and relate where it finds experts to the size of the region measured in Section F.7.

Experimental setup. For each model we draw 300300 perturbed models at each noise size, 6 sizes for GSM8K, the task of Gan and Isola (2026), and 3 for each of the 9 behaviors of the setup (5 GSM8K sizes for Tulu-3-8B-SFT, and 3 and 2 for the Qwen2.5-7B base model), with the sizes placed per model in units of the displacement they cause in the hidden state. Each perturbed model is scored on a selection split of 3232 items, and the 2020 best are scored again on a disjoint held-out split of 6464 items. A perturbed model is an expert when it still answers fluently (distinct-2 of at least 0.50.5) and gains at least 0.100.10 over the base model on the held-out split. For each model, task and seed, the expert fraction is the share of the 2020 re-scored models that are experts, at the noise size with the highest mean share over the other two seeds of the same model and task, so that the size is never chosen on the seed it is read on.

Where the search finds experts. On GSM8K the expert fraction is 0.200.20 on average over the 18 models. It is highest on Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen3.5-9B (0.870.87 each) and the Qwen2.5-7B base model (0.680.68), followed by Qwen3.5-4B (0.380.38), Qwen2.5-7B (0.250.25), Llama-3.1-8B (0.220.22), Tulu-3-8B-SFT (0.180.18) and Qwen3.6-27B (0.120.12), and at most 0.030.03 on the other 10 models. On the behaviors of the setup it is 0.0130.013 on average: the search finds experts on 12 pairs of model and behavior in 8 models (copy and the conditional echo on the base models of Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen2.5-7B, the conditional echo on Qwen2.5-3B, the conditional echo and bullets on Qwen2.5-0.5B, and bullets on Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B and SmolLM2-1.7B), and none in the other models.

Experts and the size of the region. In the 18 models, the behaviors on which the search finds an expert have wider regions than those on which it finds none (Figure 44). Over the 7272 pairs of model and behavior in the 8 models where the search finds any expert, the region size separates the two at an AUC of 0.820.82 (p<0.001p<0.001) and correlates with the expert fraction at Spearman +0.43+0.43 (p<0.001p<0.001). Over all pairs in the 18 models, the same values are 0.790.79 and +0.27+0.27 (p<0.001p<0.001 each). Split into quartiles of region area, the search finds an expert in 0%0\% of the pairs of the narrowest quartile (mean area 0.290.29), then in 3%3\% and 10%10\%, and in 17%17\% of the widest (mean area 0.710.71). The 12 expert pairs have regions covering 0.390.39 to 0.850.85 of the grid, and French, pirate and grumpy critic, the three behaviors with the narrowest regions, hold no expert in any model.

Relation to trained states. We compare the experts on GSM8K with a shift adapter trained on GSM8K, and the two arrive at the same state. Their fields point the same way: over the 328328 experts, the median cosine between an expert’s field and the trained adapter’s field is 0.230.23. They solve the same problems: of the held-out problems an expert solves beyond the base model, the trained adapter solves 1.361.36 times as many as chance would give, and more than chance for 91%91\% of the experts (Figure 45a). A shift adapter trained on an expert’s answers keeps 48%48\% of the experts’ improvement, measured on a separate split of GSM8K that played no part in selecting the experts (a ratio of sums over the 328328 experts distilled), where the same training on the trained adapter’s own answers keeps 92%92\% (Figure 45b).
